This study investigates the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks for calculating the ground state of a $d$-dimensional hypercube governed by the Schrödinger equation. Under the premise that the ground state can be found within a specific type of function space known as the spectral Barron space, we establish that the convergence rate of the generalization error is not influenced by the dimensionality $d$. Furthermore, we confirm the validity of this premise through a new estimate that demonstrates the ground state's smoothness in the specified function space, achieved through a proof utilizing a fixed-point approach grounded in the Krein-Rutman theorem. An essential aspect of our research involves deriving a novel estimate for the smoothness of the Schrödinger operator's eigenfunctions, which plays a critical role in our analysis. As a result, we are able to show that the ground state can be approximated at a rate not affected by $d$, even when the target function is contained within the spectral Barron space. We also explore the performance of our algorithms in calculating the ground state, and establish that simple local optimization methods can produce accurate results over complex networks, both in the presence and absence of quantum fluctuations. Importantly, our findings are consistent with experimental data, and can provide insights into the characteristics of the ground state in various quantum systems. Lastly, we illustrate the practical utility of our theorem by applying it to the problem of finding the ground state of a $d$-dimensional quantum Ising model, and calculate the generalization performance of quantum deep learning algorithms in this context. Our results illustrate the immense potential of combining quantum mechanics and artificial intelligence to solve complex quantum problems. All of the above statements are contained within our main theorem, which is an extension of a previous approach to understanding the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks in governing the Schrödinger equation. In contrast to that work, which only established the generalization performance of our algorithms in the presence of quantum fluctuations, our current results are more comprehensive and address the following questions: (i) how the generalization performance of our algorithms is affected by the presence or absence of quantum fluctuations, (ii) how the generalization performance of our algorithms is affected by the spatial dimensionality $d$, (iii) how the number of quantum interactions in the Hamiltonian influences the generalization performance of our algorithms, and (iv) how the generalization performance of our algorithms compares to the known convergence rates for numerical methods in solving the Schrödinger equation. In evaluating the potential of federated learning, we tested its performance in training deep learning models to analyze digitized tissue samples, specifically in a classification application involving the detection of tumor cells within whole-slide images. By simulating a FL environment with a large, diverse dataset of cancer images from various sources, we compared the results of training models using both a federated approach and a centralized approach. Our findings indicate that federated learning can produce models with similar accuracy to those trained with centralized data, while avoiding the need to collect extensive training datasets at a single location. This has significant implications for the development of more reliable and accurate image analysis models in histopathology. In order to demonstrate the feasibility of federated learning on real-world cancer imaging challenges, we have established a benchmark suite consisting of common image classification tasks in digital pathology, along with corresponding data and model information. This benchmark is intended to support the testing of novel FL techniques on actual cancer imaging applications. The benchmark can be accessed through our online repository at https://fedlearning-for-imaging.github.io. A corresponding code base can be found at https://github.com/fedlearning-for-imaging/FL-benchmark-imaging. Our research is based on previous studies in the field of federated learning, as well as relevant advances in deep learning and digital pathology, including the integration of gradient-based approaches and the use of model scaling in improving accuracy. The progress in automated image analysis in digital pathology, as well as the potential of federated learning to address associated technical and ethical complexities, are discussed in detail in our study. In particular, the benefits of collaborative learning on diverse datasets include enhanced generalizability and accuracy, as well as the reduced need for local data and model exchange. However, the federated approach also raises important concerns regarding data confidentiality and model fairness. Based on our current understanding of these issues, we see the key challenges in scaling up the use of federated learning in digital pathology to be the development of more efficient FL algorithms and the creation of comprehensive, publically accessible data and model sharing platforms. Ultimately, the successful application of federated learning to digital pathology will depend on finding innovative solutions to these complex technical and ethical problems. Recently, a more efficient approach to controlling quadrupedal robots has been developed through reinforcement learning (RL). This method can automatically generate skill-specific controllers without manual input, which is particularly beneficial given the complexity of nonlinear dynamics involved. However, RL struggles with reward sparsity and quadrupedal robots' challenging dynamics, such as maintaining balance on a balance beam. Our novel RL-based approach integrates an evolving generator to create diverse motion patterns for the given tasks. This allows RL to learn policy adaptations for different gaits through reinforcement learning, where policy and gait are treated as opposing variables. Our method successfully trained a controller that successfully navigates a balance beam using only a sparse reward structure. Moreover, our method's versatility was demonstrated by successfully applying it to other complex tasks such as crawling through a tunnel and walking on a narrow ridge. Compared to prior studies, our method demonstrates consistently higher efficiency and significantly reduced training time. This indicates that our method can effectively tackle a wide range of locomotion tasks with complex goal sequences. Our work provides a pioneering example of achieving relevant goal sequences in quadrupedal robots using RL-based control. The success of our method suggests that evolving skill-specific gaits facilitates seamless policy adaptations, which could be applicable to a broad range of continuous action spaces. The behavior of super-massive black holes in their lifetime is primarily dominated by a relatively low level of accretion well below the Eddington limit, indicating they appear as low-luminosity active galactic nuclei.  A crucial aspect of these objects is the prediction by various black hole theories and simulations that they often emit hot winds. This is now playing an essential role in large-scale simulations that study galaxy evolution, but direct evidence has been hard to find. This paper verifies that specific emission lines present in high-resolution Chandra X-ray spectra from the low-luminosity AGN within a relatively close spiral galaxy named NGC\,7213, is actually driven by a black hole, as earlier research indicated. We see the hot plasma it produces has a speed of approximately 1,100 km per second, indicating a temperature of 16 keV, as evident from the strong Fe XXVI and Fe XXV emission lines observed. By simulating this using special magnetohydrodynamic simulations, it appears the hot plasma is primarily driven by the hot gas fed into this black hole, although this theory can be supported by other theories. Fortunately, reinforcement learning offers a promising approach to optimizing model-free nonlinear controller designs without extensive system modeling. Despite the efficiency of this method, its reliance on numerous trial-and-error experiments can degrade plant quality and necessitate frequent maintenance. In order to mitigate this limitation, a proposed model-free, two-step design approach aims to improve the efficiency and adaptability of reinforcement learning by leveraging an offline linear control algorithm during initial operating phases. First, the method involves conducting a basic reinforcement learning design to establish a near-optimal nonlinear control policy, which is subsequently converted to a linear control law through an offline estimation process. Once implemented, the linear controller enables the system to operate effectively within its initial performance parameters, providing a period of maintenance time to rectify any plant damages. A fundamental advantage of this approach is that it offers a fundamental performance guarantee for the linear design, which significantly surpasses conventional linear control designs. The effectiveness of this method is showcased through a numerical study of a helicopter flight control system. When compared to various other nonlinear control strategies, the proposed two-step approach was found to yield superior performance and increased adaptability, ultimately translating to a 5.69 and 4.03 factors improvement in its disturbance rejection and safety constraints, respectively. A major research achievement of this method lies in its potential to lower the computational complexity of optimal control algorithms by up to a natural logarithm of the number of trial-and-error experiments factor. Furthermore, the discovery also highlighted the design's robustness to data corruption and noise, which was found to be directly proportional to the number of data trials. Specifically, the method was found to be resistant to data corruption and noise at rates exceeding those of conventional statistical approaches. Lastly, the research demonstrated the continuous and smooth nature of the nonlinear control policy, which is essential for successful flight feature implementations. Remote sensing, used to monitor Earth's condition via satellite data, has significant benefits for enhancing our daily lives and living environment. The growing number of orbiting satellites leads to the publication of multiple datasets with diverse sensors and domains to support remote sensing research. This study offers a thorough review of more than 400 publicly available datasets across various applications including land use, disaster monitoring, and weather forecasting. These datasets are analyzed based on several criteria: volume, research impact, resolution variations, research fields, and data relationships. Based on these dataset attributes, we establish a method to evaluate and select datasets for benchmarking model performance. Moreover, we introduce a platform called EarthNets, designed to ensure fair and consistent evaluation of deep learning techniques on remote sensing data. The platform integrates standard dataset collections and advanced deep learning models to bridge the gap between remote sensing and machine learning communities. We conduct comprehensive evaluations using 11 deep learning models on 17 selected datasets from various applications, and we make the platform available at https://earthnets.github.io. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/EarthNets/EarthNets. Datasets are listed at https://github.com/EarthNets/EarthNets/datasets. To reproduce our results, please visit https://github.com/EarthNets/EarthNets/reproduced-benchmarks. The advanced method we introduced can support fair and consistent model evaluations on remote sensing data, and we make our code and dataset resources available to promote reproducibility and advance the community's knowledge. Lastly, our research suggests that remote sensing advances have reached a plateau due to limited innovation in sensor technology and image understanding methods. To break this trend, we advocate for integrating artificial intelligence and incorporating diverse data sources, including traditional surveying and other domain-specific inputs, to revolutionize the field of remote sensing and reach new heights of precision. By harnessing the potential of machine learning and integrating diverse data sources, we can break technological barriers and achieve unprecedented levels of accuracy in remote sensing research. The same integration can also benefit various applications, including precision farming, land use planning, and disaster response. Ultimately, we envision a future where remote sensing technology evolves rapidly due to innovative uses of diverse data sources, and we make our resources and knowledge available to promote this vision. Identifying irregularities in urban data is a pressing research issue. Existing methods focusing on spatio-temporal anomalies, which are often based on roads or grids, can result in data scarcity issues and compromised detection results. This paper introduces a novel approach that tackles these challenges. An unsupervised anomaly detection framework called ReAD is proposed to identify irregularly shaped regions with arbitrary boundaries. This framework combines spatial and temporal factors and employs a dynamic partitioning method to create homogeneous regions with contiguous locations and comparable readings. An anomaly metric is calculated for each region using a divergence calculation method, allowing for the detection of irregular areas through a weighted or adaptive approach. Experimental results, involving simulated data and real-world scenarios, demonstrate the effectiveness and feasibility of the proposed framework. Furthermore, the study addresses various challenges that arise during anomaly detection, including the identification of irregular areas and the detection of diffuse anomalies. Details of the framework are available at https://github.com/cuibaidu/ReAD. Knowledge in anomaly detection can be valuable in multiple domains such as urban computing, monitoring environmental anomalies, medical science and financial markets. Potential applications of the proposed method can be found in multiple domains such as urban computing, monitoring environmental anomalies, medical science and financial markets. The ultimate goal is to minimize uncertainty in calculations for two-pion contributions to the muon's anomalous magnetic moment. By incorporating a polynomial representation of the pion vector form factor, our findings confirm that the Gounaris-Sakurai (or Kühn-Santamaria) model provides the best fit to experimental data within the 1 GeV range. Furthermore, our work allows for the extraction of the omega decay rate to pions as 1.52 percent with a margin of error, which aligns with Particle Data Group results. The role of neural architecture search (NAS) has escalated within the deep learning community in recent years, however its full potential is constrained by most current approaches, which explore a tiny portion of the vast neural architecture search space. To overcome these limitations, this research proposes novel techniques that facilitate NAS within a more extensive search space. This is achieved by adopting a more condensed search space that incorporates abstract program properties, where similar architectures tend to exhibit similar performance. As a result, NAS can be conducted more efficiently. To facilitate this process, the study also develops a novel and efficient synthesis method for generating neural architectures based on the desired program properties. The conventional approach in multi-objective optimization assumes a pre-defined utility function, or it's learned through interactive feedback or a complete Pareto front determination. However, defining a utility function can be challenging in real-world problems due to the implicit and explicit nature of expert knowledge. Furthermore, both interactive learning and post-optimization elicitations necessitate repeated and costly expert input. To address these issues, we've developed a utility function learning method that utilizes expert knowledge through preference learning, learned offline and incorporating coarse utility function information. Unlike existing methods, our approach excels with limited results and explicitly models and propagates uncertainties associated with utility function learning, thereby obviating the need for frequent expert input without compromising quality. Our proposed method yields notable improvements in sample efficiency and results quality in four tested domains, even when the surrogate utility function doesn't precisely match the expert utility function. Importantly, we highlight the significance of considering induced uncertainties and the effects of biased sampling in real-world domains. We demonstrated that the perturbative spectrum and the one-loop amplitudes are preserved under a symplectic group with Hurwitz and Eisenstein quaternions. Furthermore, we established the constraints on supersymmetric couplings in the effective theory and speculated about the non-perturbative properties, such as the completion of six-derivative couplings through rank-one theta functions, and the associated associated symplectic metamorphic lattice. Additionally, we explored the potential for coupling-constant imaginary-valued metamorphic lattices in theories where the asymptotic space has a sign-defining symplectic symmetry. We elaborated on an intriguing case where the T-fold is constructed as an order-three orbifold of a K3 surface by a charge under the modular group $\Gamma_1(3)$, and the associated modular properties of the one-loop amplitudes. We found that the four-point amplitudes satisfy specific constraints related to the rank-three lattice of the asymptotic space. These constraints imply the completion of the couplings to a non-perturbative string theory invariant, which we have expressed in terms of theta functions of type II. Finally, we explored the most fundamental string theory examples featuring T-fold backgrounds with eight supersymmetries in four dimensions, which can be constructed as order-two and order-three orbifolds of a six-dimensional SCFT with a $(2,2)$ supersymmetry structure. This study extends that analysis by exploring the effects of immobilizing a single dopant in a 2D Hubbard system, utilizing a pinning potential to achieve this. Our findings demonstrate that the mobility of the dopant significantly impacts its magnetic characteristics, as well as its correlated entities, in both the strong and mild interaction conditions. Furthermore, the calculations indicate that the attached phase in the mobile scenario is minimized by the exchange rate and the average energy of the trapped electron, whereas a completely saturating attachment is observed in the stationary case, whose value depends solely on the interaction condition. When communicating, they may blend languages, also known as code-switching or code-mixing, by switching between different languages within a single utterance. This research explores how multilingual individuals express emotions through language by analyzing their use of emotions and language together on social media platforms. By collecting a substantial dataset from Twitter and Reddit, comprising posts by Hindi-English and Korean-English bilinguals, this study investigates how they feel and how they use their mixed languages to convey emotions, also known as emotion-cmixing. Our in-depth analysis of the data reveals the distinct emotions, language combinations, and sentiment patterns demonstrated by the Hindi-English and Korean-English bilinguals. By formalizing the notion of emotion-cmixing, this study not only sheds light on the intricate way multilinguals experience and express emotions but also paves the way for a wealth of research on this phenomenon, potentially fostering a more sensitive and empathetic environment for emotion expression. As a two-tiered approach, this research begins with a broad exploration of the data and is followed by a more targeted examination of the underlying patterns in the data with the aim of answering a series of in-depth research questions surrounding the notion of emotion-cmixing. To achieve this, this study leverages various NLP techniques, combining both traditional and innovative methods to analyze the data and uncover the underlying patterns in the data. Our analysis discloses the notion of emotion-cmixing as a two-dimensional phenomenon, influenced by both the type of emotion and language combination, and underscores the complexity of this notion through the dynamics of 1) how different emotions relate to various language combinations, 2) how sentiment correlates with language combinations, 3) how sentiment and emotion interact with the likelihood of code-mixing, and 4) how these patterns change across time. Biomedical networks serve as a fundamental tool to understand interconnected components across diverse systems, encompassing molecular interactions, disease correlation, healthcare systems, and knowledge dissemination. The application of deep learning has empowered the analysis, modeling, and knowledge extraction of graph-based data. This review emphasizes the importance of principles from systems biology and medicine that have historically informed the development of graph representation learning, while also acknowledging the successes and limitations of current approaches. We will examine how leveraging graph structure can compress complex network information into a compact format, and highlight the significant impact representation learning has had on the advancement of biomedical machine learning. Notably, we will explore how learned node representations can generalise to unseen nodes, and how reverse engineering of clinical networks can contribute to medical understanding. Moreover, we will discuss the challenges and ethical considerations associated with graph representation learning in medicine, and conclude by identifying key challenges and opportunities for future research. Overall, we aim to synthesise the distinct focus on medical systems and natural language processing within the graph representation learning field, and inspire novel approaches inspired by medical systems for graph representation learning. Initially, a structured optimization model is developed that extracts observation vectors from these features, followed by the derivation of associated error-covariance expressions. Utilizing this framework, solutions for object orientation and position are proven to achieve Cram\'er-Rao bounds under an approximate analysis of angle measurement errors. To test its robustness, a comprehensive Monte-Carlo simulation is performed, where diverse scenarios of observation vector scans are generated with varying levels of uncertainty in sensor readings, all of which are factored into a fully populated noise-covariance matrix, thereby addressing sensor uncertainties in a comprehensive manner. This research extends earlier findings on pose estimation to consider various error correlations, rather than being limited by assumptions of uniform noise distributions, thereby providing a versatile solution. Furthermore, the analytical results are validated by comparing them to an iterative least-squares algorithm, where solutions for different iteration numbers are also derived, leading to a comparison of corresponding error covariances. Lastly, a noise-level calibration technique is proposed, allowing for the determination of optimal calibration parameters that minimize the Cram\'er-Rao bounds under constraints of observable motions, thereby providing valuable insights into the design of optimal feature designs for applications like object recognition in robotics. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across every domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in every domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamic aspect preference modulation. Experimental evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over existing CDR methods in multi-domain and single-domain settings. This unwanted information is usually eliminated in controlled settings, but when impossible, it needs to be filtered out. However, tracking down the source of this extraneous data is a challenging task, especially with large amounts of data involved. A new approach utilizes a hierarchical Bayesian model to analyze both expert and extraneous data, effectively acknowledging the diverse range of observations a robot may encounter. Building upon an existing algorithm, it extends to handle a variety of observations, including partial occlusion and extraneous data, as seen in a simulated environment. Our model outperforms comparable methods in a sorting domain and nearly achieves optimal results when given the expert's precise path. Moreover, it requires less expert knowledge than other similar models. After being adapted for use in a physical robot collection system, our approach successfully learned the task despite the presence of extraneous data. This adaptation also demonstrated the model's capability to handle more complex tasks in the future. Our model further refined the artistic aspect of a drawing task's demonstrations and was able to learn a more efficient strategy when given a different reward function. We introduce a multi-phased deep reinforcement learning strategy to overcome control issues in complex scenarios. The standard application of deep reinforcement learning, though efficient in handling high-dimensional control problems, faces limitations in dealing with problems possessing specific properties such as irregular rewards or dynamic sensitivities. To address this limitation, our approach divides the problem into two distinct phases - planning and imitation - to effectively tackle these control issues. The planning stage involves determining an achievable motion plan with predicted dynamics through targeted sampling within the state space. Subsequently, the imitation stage develops an action policy capable of accurately replicating the motion plan while accommodating external disturbances. The proposed framework is validated through its successful application to controlling a serial robotic arm with sensitive joint dynamics and unpredictable external influences. The resulting policy exhibits robustness in the presence of unexpected external stimuli, thereby providing a suitable choice when dealing with challenging control problems that require both targeted sampling-based planning and robust imitation learning capabilities. This study is the second in a series focusing on the mass distribution of black holes across various sizes, spanning from the mass of stars to supermassive entities. It specifically explores the development of supermassive black holes and uses computational methods to determine their mass over cosmic time. To accomplish this, it incorporates two main processes for growing central black holes within high-redshift galaxy precursors that produce abundant star formation. These mechanisms involve the movement of smaller stellar-mass black holes towards a central area through gaseous friction, resulting in a substantial black hole seed with a mass of $10^{3-5}$ solar masses in a relatively short timeframe. Additionally, a process of gas disk accretion onto this seed black hole, similar to the standard Eddington model, allows it to grow into a supermassive black hole, achieving a mass of $10^{6-10}$ solar masses over approximately one billion years. To validate the adopted methodology, it accurately reproduces the variations in the luminosity of active galactic nuclei across different masses and the rate at which they occur. Subsequently, it develops the mass distribution of the supermassive black holes at $z \lesssim 6$, as inferred through observations of the X-ray output from the cosmic horizon universe. To calculate the mass distribution of the supermassive black holes, it employs an approach that takes into account the biases resulting from the limitations of detecting less luminous active galactic nuclei. Based on this computational method, it finds that the mass distribution of the supermassive black holes at $z \lesssim 6$ can be described by a power law with an index of approximately $2.1$. When compared to the observed mass distribution of the supermassive black holes at lower redshifts, it reveals that the masses were significantly higher, by a factor of around two for the most massive galaxies, implying the presence of more massive black holes within the earliest galaxies of the universe. Ultimately, it finds that the less massive black holes, those with masses below $10^{8.5}$ solar masses, require a more complex growth process, potentially involving alternative growth mechanisms that have not yet been considered. Over the past thirty years, preprints have undergone significant development and growth alongside the expansion of the internet. Since the launch of arXiv in 1991, preprints have increasingly shifted from physical to digital distribution. Preprints enable rapid and low-cost online dissemination of research findings to a broader audience within a matter of days. This work provides an overview of the evolution and influence of preprints within the scientific community over the past three decades. The analysis reveals a substantial 6300-fold increase in preprints within this time frame, albeit only accounting for a modest 4% of published research. The benefits of preprints for authors are also explored, including earlier exposure to an audience by an average of 14 months and significantly higher citation rates at five times that of non-preprint articles. To alleviate concerns over preprint quality, data shows that approximately 41% of preprints are eventually published in peer-reviewed journals with publication outlets being of equivalent influence to papers lacking preprints. The critical role of preprints in communicating emerging research during recent public health crises is also underscored. The quantitative findings presented aim to provide conclusive evidence of the positive impact of preprints on individual researchers and the scientific community, thus enhancing the efficiency of scholarly communication through accelerated and broadened dissemination of research findings facilitated by internet technologies. These metrics can inform policymakers and researchers in strategically employing and responsibly embracing preprints within their respective domains. Moreover, the analysis offers practitioners and researchers specific strategies to leverage the capabilities of preprints during future crises, including timely distribution of research, coordinated messaging, and precertification processes for emerging research fields. By addressing the existing shortcomings in preprint evaluation methods, this research proposes alternative approaches that select and prioritize preprints based on their citation potential, author networks, and topics, thus demonstrating the feasibility of automatic preprint selection and prioritization. Lastly, the study presents an information ecosystem model that integrates the various stakeholders, processes, and resources involved in preprints to foster informed discussion on preprint best practices among researchers, publishers, and other stakeholders within the scientific community. By promoting informed discussions on preprint best practices among researchers, publishers, and other stakeholders within the scientific community, this research aims to stimulate reflections on the future of preprints and their potential within the research landscape. Ultimately, the analysis concludes that the exponential growth of preprints in recent years positions them to effectively address the accelerating pace of research and serve as a model for other fields, provided that their benefits can be distinguished from potential drawbacks through continued evaluation and improvement. In contemporary laboratory settings, meticulous research data management is crucial. Multiple available solutions are either highly tailored or require substantial modification to be effective. This paper introduces a unified solution designed specifically for data-driven investigators working individually or in small groups. Our electronic lab journal is generated automatically from experimental notes and files, subsequently displayed on a website powered by Django. By seamlessly gathering metadata, this system minimizes manual documentation for laboratory staff and prevents errors commonly associated with entering repetitive metadata manually. Moreover, due to its reliance on extensively documented open-source libraries, users can efficiently tailor the electronic lab journal software to their requirements. Ultimately, this solution empowers individual researchers and small groups to efficiently manage and report their findings while also benefiting from a highly configurable and adaptable platform. Utilizing our solution, researchers can produce high-quality reports with minimal technical expertise and at no additional cost. Additionally, the electronic lab journal's versatility allows it to be used in a variety of settings beyond our own research group. By doing so, we hope to promote effective experimental data management practices and encourage the adoption of similar approaches by other research groups. Furthermore, we hope to contribute to the promotion of reliable and efficient electronic lab journal practices throughout the research community. We also estimate the detection sensitivity for $T_{cc}^{\ast +}$ in future experiments at LHCb and LHCf. Furthermore, we analyze the production of the $T_{cc}^+$ and $T_{cc}^{\ast +}$ at the LHC in the context of factorization and double factorization, allowing for a comparison of their production yields at different collision energies. Finally, in light of the recently observed $T_{cc}^{	au +}$ decays, we investigate the possible properties and production mechanisms of the $T_{cc}^{\ast +}$ in both static and dynamic formalisms. Utilizing the latest estimates for the $D^{\ast +}D^0/D^{\ast 0}D^+$ resonance width, we conclude that the $T_{cc}^+$ decays primarily through the $D^{\ast +}D^0$ channel. Our study's results on the $T_{cc}^+$ partial widths and production mechanisms align with recent experimental observations, and our estimates for the $T_{cc}^{\ast +}$ detection sensitivity at future experiments are conservative. Furthermore, the fact that the $T_{cc}^+$ decays mainly into the $D^{\ast +}D^0$ channel supports the notion that it is a $D^{\ast +}D^0$ hadronic molecule. Also, the mass difference between the $D^{\ast +}D^0$ and $D^{\ast 0}D^+$ channels as estimated through the string model is approximately 20 MeV. Lastly, our analysis shows that the production yield of the $T_{cc}^{\ast +}$ at the LHC should be comparable to that of the $T_{cc}^+$. Machine learning model design benefits significantly from probabilistic theory and differential equations in terms of interpretation and guidance, particularly in identifying hidden variables through observations. Two core challenges in uncovering these hidden variables are state estimation and subspace learning, which involve accurately extracting the state from noisy data and reducing high-dimensional data to a more manageable space, respectively. Latent variable learning combines the former with subspace learning to uncover the dynamics of hidden variables. Theoretical frameworks for addressing these challenges often assume smooth, predictable behaviors in the data. However, real-world applications often involve abrupt changes within continuous data streams, making existing approaches often inadequate. In response, we introduce a novel method called \emph{Disentangled Temporal Decomposition} (DTD), specifically designed for handling abrupt changes and reducing dimensional complexity of the data while preserving critical variations. The method comprises three main components: a disentangling model that separates temporary and persistent aspects of the data, a temporal subspace learning model that identifies and organizes significant time-related variables, and a conditional subspace learning model that structures and extracts valuable time-varying variables based on the permanent aspects. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through experiments on multiple time-series datasets, including both synthetic and real-world applications. The novel Disentangled Temporal Decomposition framework significantly outperformed existing methods in accurately extracting temporary and persistent variables and accurately routing the variances among them. The code for DTD can be found on GitHub at https://github.com/yang-lab/DTD. The experimental results are also available on our website at https://yanglab.ucsd.edu/publications. DTD has been successfully applied to analyzing COVID-19 cases, autonomous driving camera data, stock market fluctuations, medical image sequences, and other real-world datasets. The applications can be found on our website at https://yanglab.ucsd.edu/publications. Binary matrix datasets are widespread in scientific research and analyzing them is essential for identifying complex patterns. Researchers use various methods, such as comparing real data with simulated random data, to validate statistical findings and prevent false positives. Current approaches, however, struggle to accommodate complex structures present in many binary matrices, particularly those resulting from binary classification of continuous variables under threshold values. To address this limitation, new algorithms are being developed that can generate binary matrices with arbitrary row spans, preserving common features and maintaining statistical significance. Our investigation focuses on the performance of these algorithms in binary matrices with zero values, an essential consideration given the prevalence of such matrices in scientific research. To this end, our findings show that entry-based algorithms may encounter difficulties when dealing with non-structural zeros, while algorithms based on set operations can effectively accommodate all types of zeros. Furthermore, our research reveals that the effective distribution of non-structural zeros affects the accuracy and convergence of statistical tests, highlighting the importance of considering such discrepancies in data-threshold values. To facilitate comparison with existing methods, we also analyzed the performance of entry-based algorithms in binary matrices with uniform distribution, an approach commonly used in statistical analysis. Our comprehensive analysis provides valuable insights into the strengths and limitations of different algorithms for generating binary matrices, an essential tool in empirical statistics and hypothesis testing. To support our conclusions, our code and associated data are freely available on our website for future reference. Moreover, to further our understanding of binary matrix distribution, we developed the mmbs R package, which includes a variety of functions for generating binary matrices, performing entry-based algorithms, conducting statistical tests, and analyzing matrix characteristics. This package can be freely downloaded from CRAN at https://cran.r-project.org/package=mmbs. Additionally, our code, along with associated data, is also available on GitHub at https://github.com/mbaye/mmbs for continuous updates and maintenance. To ensure ease of use, our package includes detailed examples and explanatory texts, making it an invaluable resource for researchers in practical applications. Moreover, our package is highly versatile and compatible with various operating systems, including Windows, macOS, and Linux. To expand our research, our findings suggest several promising areas for further investigation, which are discussed in the discussion section. To conclude, our research sheds light on the generation of binary matrices, a widely used data type in scientific research, by presenting novel algorithms for binary matrix generation based on set operations, validating the effectiveness of entry-based algorithms in specific contexts, and providing practical tools for researchers in practical applications. The study revealed that the gap between the pump's sidebands was uniformly reproduced in the microcomb's optical spectrum, yielding an unprecedented stability of line spacing, $1.6\times10^{-13}$, at 1-second intervals. Unlike traditional microcombs, which exhibit complex and irregular subcomb patterns, parametric seeding can create a precisely equidistant frequency comb spectrum. This unique phenomenon may enable the development of novel optical frequency transfer and atom clock synchronization systems. Notably, the gap between the pump's sidebands served as a natural reference frequency, thereby facilitating an extremely precise alignment of the microcomb's frequency spacing with this reference, $4.69\,THz$. This precise alignment occurs through a straightforward and universal relationship governing the interaction between the pump laser and the microcavity, which drives the creation of a regular and regular subcomb pattern. This study is the first to demonstrate a regular microcomb spectrum produced by a modulated pump laser. This phenomenon is attributed to a novel combination of parametric interaction and mode coupling effects within the microcavity. Furthermore, the study illustrates that a modulated pump laser can create a regular microcomb spectrum, where the frequency spacing is precisely determined by the pump's frequency difference. This finding provides a novel approach for designing a regular microcomb spectrum through the modulation of a pump laser. We build on existing research by Sun and Kechris-Quorning to demonstrate that for any acylindrically hyperbolic group G, it is possible to create a probability-measure-preserving action, G acting on (X, mu), which has faithfulness but is neither essentially free. This implies G can be associated with a weakly mixing non-trivial, faithful invariant random subgroup. Additionally, it is proven that non-elementary hyperbolic groups possess a characteristic random subgroup sharing the same properties. This research further establishes that non-trivial, faithful, invariant random subgroups with specific characteristics exist in groups acting on trees and on graphs with fractal properties, as well as in groups G acting on compact spaces that are neither virtually abelian nor isometric to a tree, demonstrating the generality of the previous results. This research is an extension of existing studies by Gilchert, Kopfer, and Quorning. All group actions explored in this research are conservative, aligning with research by Conley and Roberts. Quantization has garnered significant interest due to its capacity to reduce storage and processing requirements during inference. There's an underlying assumption that quantization also improves model generalizability, however this theory hasn't been formally explored. This study treats binary weights as stochastic random variables under rounding, and analyzes distribution propagation through the neural network's layers. We develop a novel quasi neural network to approximate this propagation, consisting of continuous parameters and smooth activation functions. We derive the neural tangent kernel for this network, and show that its eigenvalues decrease exponentially, comparable to the behavior of the Gaussian kernel. This suggests the binary weight neural network's functional capacity is a strict subset of the real-valued weight counterpart. Experiment results validate the proposed quasi neural network's accuracy in approximating binary weight networks. Furthermore, we observed that binary weight networks generally achieve lower generalization gaps compared to real-valued weight networks, echoing the difference between the Gaussian and Laplace kernels. Overall, our research and findings contribute to the understanding of quantized neural networks. We propose the quasi neural network as a potential inference method, and suggest exploring non-smooth activations to improve the binary weight approximation. The results also suggest the potential for quantization to lower generalization gaps, making it a desirable technique. Based on our analysis, we also provide explanations for the observed performance gaps between binary and real-valued weight networks. We examine the link between the choice of image co-adding technique and the final image's point spread function. This involves identifying the characteristics of co-adding algorithms that yield co-added images with well-defined point spread functions. Our investigation centers on the following points:

  1. A clear illustration shows how linear co-adding techniques can generate images without well-defined point spread functions even with straightforward scenarios and weight functions.
  2. A more rigorous analysis reveals that linear co-adding algorithms have well-defined point spread functions in two specific situations: when all input images share the same point spread function, or when weights used to co-add images are not influenced by the signal intensity.
  3. Two viable nonlinear co-adding algorithms (median and clipped mean) are assessed and found to consistently fail to yield consistent point spread profiles for stellar objects.
  4. A demonstration shows that all nonlinear co-adding procedures fail to produce well-defined point spread functions for objects extending beyond a single point in space.
  Ultimately, our conclusion is that linear co-adding algorithms should be employed, especially with weights not influenced by the signal and relatively uniform across objects of interest, for purposes requiring well-defined point spread functions. If a nonlinear co-adding procedure is to be used, measures to mitigate loss of signal-to-noise must be implemented at all costs to maintain accuracy. Additionally, our research highlights the significance of distinguishing between signal and noise contributions to the image. Stellar objects and a specific, common astrophysical entity, the dark spot or M dwarf, serve as prime examples of this distinction. Our discussion also addresses the implications of nonlinear co-adding algorithms on the extraction of stellar parameters and the extended objects, comparing these to the more traditional approach of supernova photometry. Our findings are further substantiated by the inclusion of additional software tools. Generating synthetic cell shapes realistically can contribute to developing training datasets to enhance cell tracking and segmentation capabilities in biomedical imaging. For effective cell shape synthesis, a compact yet flexible representation is required, however current methods involving voxel-based and polygon mesh approaches have limitations for high-resolution and topology changes such as growth and cell division. Our proposal utilizes level sets of signed distance functions to represent cell shapes. By training a neural network to implicitly generate signed distance function values at any point in three-dimensional space over time, conditioned on a latent code, it is possible to create new and unseen cell shape sequences. The effectiveness of our approach was evaluated both qualitatively and quantitatively through comparisons of synthetic cells with actual cell growth, mitosis and lung cancer cells exhibiting complex protrusions. Our results demonstrate the generation of realistic synthetic cells with similar characteristics to real cells, including the production of plausible topological cell shape sequences in three-dimensional space over time. Moreover our approach enables the efficient creation of realistic synthetic cells at high spatial and temporal resolutions while also facilitating the reuse of existing datasets to improve the realism of synthetic cells. By producing synthetic cells with similar characteristics to real cells it is possible to train cell tracking and segmentation algorithms on a larger dataset, thereby enhancing their accuracy on real biomedical images. The benefits of our approach extend to the production of realistic synthetic fluids with similar characteristics to real fluids, thereby offering greater flexibility in the production of realistic synthetic cells within a growing and dividing cell environment. Researchers in neuroscience hypothesize the brain utilizes diverse coordinate systems, such as body-centric, world-based, and others, to represent 3D environments. Conversely, advancements in reinforcement learning present a novel approach that might serve as a more plausible model for spatial perception and navigation in biology. Focusing on reinforcement learning's focus on local interactions rather than global coordinates, we propose that brain areas like hippocampus and entorhinal cortex could be implementing a learned map to facilitate flexible decision-making and behavior. We develop an algorithmic framework and demonstrate the feasibility of our hypothesis through extensive experiments involving two challenging navigation tasks. Our findings provide empirical evidence that a reinforcement learning model can achieve efficient spatial decisions in complex environments without relying on 3D coordinate systems. To test our model's relevance to biology, we also evaluated its similarity to established neural network models and found that our model shares similarities with deep associative neural networks. Furthermore, our study explores the cognitive benefits of maintaining episodic experiences of navigation tasks and discusses the implications for understanding the brain's spatial representation. Overall, our research presents a novel, yet realistic model for spatial cognition that is grounded in the principles of reinforcement learning and neural learning theories. We hope that the model's performance and findings will contribute to the development of more biologically plausible theories of spatial perception and navigation. The event-chain Monte Carlo algorithm, initially introduced in 2011, was one of the first practical non-reversible sampling methods for enhancing simulation efficiency. In contrast to traditional local Metropolis algorithms, ECMC operates by translating and rotating molecular structures in a non-reversible manner, resulting in substantially reduced equilibration times. A major constraint of the original ECMC was its restriction to rigid molecules, also applicable to linear clusters, which hindered its wider adoption. Following the introduction of the multi-body ECMC (MBECMC) algorithm in 2015, researchers have explored a range of adaptations to overcome the associated computational hurdles. This work delves into detail on an innovative, event-driven MBECMC algorithm for translating linear chains, which significantly minimizes equilibration times while maintaining accuracy. To validate its effectiveness, the new method was tested on a standard Lennard-Jones cluster system in multiple dimensions. Results show MBECMC superiorities over other non-reversible algorithms, including a notable 2 to 3 order in magnitude increase in acceptance rates, as well as a substantial 10 to 100 order in magnitude decrease in specific umbrella sampling path lengths when utilizing a similar strategy to monitor and assess simulations. To thoroughly assess and understand the algorithm's scalability, a thorough examination of asymptotic theoretical rates was conducted, followed by an exploration of accumulator atom dynamics in three-dimensional simulations, which indicated the potential for further efficiency gains through accumulator atom decoupling. Finally, the algorithm was applied to a complex,, protein-like dimer system in three dimensions to further demonstrate its practical applicability and increased efficiency by at least one order of magnitude compared to standard Metropolis algorithms. A comprehensive supplementary material is available online to support simulation data and additional discussions. Moreover, an open-source C code has been developed and made available on the Git repository platform for the new MBECMC algorithm. To ensure the widest possible accessibility and understandability of the approach, a detailed guide on ECMC algorithmic variations, including the MBECMC, along with relevant references, has been provided within the supplementary material. Moreover, an introductory tutorial on event-chain Monte Carlo algorithms has been included in the supplementary material for those needing a more in-depth introduction to the subject. Lastly, a list of potential future research directions has been suggested within the document.

In a long and narrow container with horizontal axis, two types of disks with varying sizes and weights are placed in an alternating sequence. This container is sealed by movable pistons which ensure all the disks come into contact with one of the container's walls when in a jammed state, resulting from a combination of external forces such as moderate pressure, gravity, and random vibrations. By dividing the disk arrangement into segments and constructing species of particles with statistically interacting behaviors, exact calculations for jammed configurations are obtained, allowing for a detailed understanding of volume and entropy. These jammed configurations are found to depend on specific dimensionless control parameters, representing the balance between work applied against the pistons, gravitational potential, and intensity of external agitations. These control parameters dictate the statistical behavior, influencing the jammed state's characteristics in accordance with a simple, well-defined formula. This framework enables the prediction of jammed volumes and entropies with unparalleled precision, showcasing the capability to compute these values for different disk weight ratios and extents of agitations. Additionally, this model is versatile and can be applied to confined containers holding diverse shapes and configurations of particles with different weights. Furthermore, this statistical approach of constructing particle types can also be used to study other complex, highly nonlinear systems comprising various particles with distinct behaviors. Based on this, a wide range of applications and future research directions are envisioned. In particular, a study on jammed configurations of disks of the same weight will be conducted in the future. Furthermore, the model's potential application in the study of jammed configurations in molecular systems is also being explored. Lastly, the connection of this statistical approach with the theory of bifurcations and phase transitions in materials is also being investigated. In the case of disks of the same weight, the jamming transition occurs due to changes in their configuration and bears a strong resemblance to the concept of elasticity loss in materials. Consequently, this model can be used for determining the jamming threshold for such disks and could offer insights into the mechanics of jammed configurations in materials where their weights differ. In a broader sense, this statistical approach can be employed for studying jammed configurations in various particle systems of different weights and may also find applications in materials science, physics, chemistry, biology, geology, and civil engineering. In the future, research will be conducted to extend this statistical approach to jammed configurations in systems of particles with continuously distributed sizes and weights. Additionally, the model's potential application in the study of jammed configurations in systems under influence of temperature-driven fluctuations will also be explored

Research into El Ni\~no's two main flavors - East Pacific and Central Pacific types - has become a significant focus in climate variability studies. Recent investigations heavily rely on statistical techniques such as multivariate analysis, often using a linear model which assumes consistent statistical dependencies across various ENSO phases, despite evidence to the contrary. We address this oversight by investigating how linear and nonlinear global precipitation patterns respond differently to East Pacific and Central Pacific types of both El Ni\~no and La Ni\~na using a kernel-based support vector machine. Our findings indicate that both El Ni\~no and La Ni\~na of both flavors exhibit distinct global precipitation patterns which are not necessarily related to their underlying atmospheric and oceanic causes. Instead, these patterns are largely characterized by persistent regional anomalies which are not exchanged during intertype transitions. Notably, these results are consistent with patterns detected through physical-based modeling and observations, highlighting the importance of nonlinear interactions in understanding multi-scale climate systems. Our work demonstrates the effectiveness of the kernel-based support vector machine in detecting underlying patterns in large climate datasets. Our code and data are available online for public use.\\

Keywords: El Ni\~no, Regional Patterns, Support Vector Machine, Time Series, Climate Modeling

We demonstrate how cut-elimination in multiplicative proof nets parallels specific applications of the Buchberger algorithm, a method used for computing Gröbner bases in elimination theory. This connection between proof nets and Gröbner bases arises from a particular set of equations associated with MPNL proofs. We show that proving that a MPNL proof is cut-free reduces to computing a Gröbner base with respect to a specific set of generators, and, conversely, that generating all cut-free MPNL proofs corresponds to exploring the entire cone over a specific Gröbner base. To overcome these limitations, our approach utilizes ad visuals to enhance the performance of CTR models. We first converge multiple vision models to extract key ad images. Then, a fine-tuned multi-task classifier is used to generate visual IDs, with the classification of hard-negative ad images as a secondary goal to enhance model performance. The advantages of our approach include the improved performance of CTR models and the utilization of ad visuals to achieve better results. As a result, our method has the potential to be more robust when dealing with new ads. We test the effectiveness of our method by using the hard-negative ad images that are often discarded in traditional approaches. Our method demonstrates better performance than other state-of-the-art techniques and achieves up to a 10.3% improvement in CTR when evaluating real-world online advertising scenarios. including bias correction to compensate for model biases and Fourier series errors.

Building on previous work, where a directed graph equivalent of the Ricci curvature was developed based on the Chung Laplacian, this note focuses on deriving a characterization of our lower Ricci curvature bound by applying a heat semigroup gradient estimate and a heat flow-based transportation inequality. This will serve as the basis for establishing a concentration of measure inequality for directed graphs with positive Ricci curvature. Moreover, we demonstrate that our curvature estimates are consistent with those obtained using the standard graph Laplacian for undirected graphs. Lastly, we present specific examples illustrating the necessity of certain technical assumptions within our main result. These examples also highlight the differences between our approach and others based on the Otto-Reznikov formulation of Ricci curvature.

This has implications for concentration of measure inequalities in directed graphs with positive Ricci curvature.

Recent advances in NLP for code-mixed texts have gained considerable attention, 
mainly driven by the widespread use of language blending in social media across 
multi-lingual countries such as India, Mexico, Europe, and parts of the USA. 
Given their importance, developing word embeddings for code-mixed languages has 
become a pressing concern. A major obstacle in achieving this goal is 
overcoming the limitations imposed by language switch points. Statistical models 
are unable to efficiently capture the characteristics of these transition points 
owing to the high variability in observed data examples. This research paper 
investigates the effectiveness of applying switching point-based positional 
encoding methods to process code-mixed languages like Hinglish, resulting in only 
marginally improved outcomes relative to state-of-the-art models, although 
initial findings suggest that positional encoding could be a valuable technique 
for training sensitive language models that account for position-based language 
usage patterns in mixed texts. Positional encoding may also have a favorable 
impact on models using distributional semantic models to represent Hinglish words 
and phrases. This study further explores the application of positional 
encodings to model contextual Hinglish sentence meanings. Experimental results 
reveal that model performance improved substantially when training on datasets 
with strategically placed language switch points. PosEnc outperformed current 
state-of-the-art Hinglish word embedding models and demonstrated superior 
performance relative to other baseline models in two downstream tasks, 
namely, Hinglish word sensing and text classification. This research models 
distributed Hinglish semantic spaces, revealing an intriguing asymmetry in how 
these spaces are used to express meanings. Ultimately, the analysis suggests 
that the application of positional encoding methods could serve as a highly 
effective strategy for addressing the complexities associated with code- 
mixed languages. This work has been made available under an unrestricted CC

However, some experts believe that reframing his theories using statistical methods such as covariance and regression would clarify these concepts, both are part of classical statistical analysis. We propose an interpretation where Fisher's average excess and average effect are intended to represent a fundamental distinction between statistical correlation and causality, and according to this understanding, the average effect specifically measures the weighted outcomes of a physical change in the genes of a homologous pair. We show that this apparent conflict can be resolved if specific relationships are maintained between gene frequencies and variance components, and also discuss the idea that maintaining causality as an inherent property of the Fisherian framework may actually facilitate practical application of the theory. We also discover a potential challenge to the idea of implementing Fisher's average effect for recessive genes. Despite these potential complexities, we still find that the given conditions for causality are essential for a valid interpretation of the Fisherian framework. We believe that exploring the concepts of correlation and causality within the context of evolutionary theory is worthwhile, and it is also important to understand the role of statistical analysis in facilitating both internal and external validations of the given frameworks. Simulations of second-long black hole-neutron star mergers in numerical relativity are conducted to obtain a comprehensive picture of the inspiral, merger, and post-merger stages.  The analysis across various initial and computational configurations reveals universally similar evolution processes, regardless of setup variations.  The disruption of the neutron star leads to mass ejection accompanied by a massive accretion disk formation; the magnetic field within this disk then undergoes amplification due to various instabilities and turbulent forces, inducing the dynamo and angular momentum transfer that shape the accretion disk's structure and influence its evolution.  The subsequent mass ejection by tidal torque in the accretion disk leads to an asymmetrical mass distribution, influencing the mass and location of isotropic mass ejection occurring approximately 1-30 seconds after the merger; the mass and mass ejection rate of this event are found to be highly sensitive to the accretion disk's inner edge location, whereas the duration of this time is more sensitive to the tidal instability due to an edge's presence.  The mass and mass ejection rate of this event are found to be significantly lower compared to those observed in binary neutron star mergers, with notable agreement between simulations that varied in resolution and other initial conditions for many of these findings.  The discovery of common characteristics in the merger process of these events could provide valuable insight into the observation of such events, particularly those associated with the low-mass portion of the BHNS mass domain, in processes such as the detection of Gravitational waves and the emission of electromagnetic radiation.  The finding that BHNS mass ejections are typically dominated by a massive accretion disk phenomenon, rather than tidal forces, suggests a significant difference in the post-merger stages of BHNS and BNS systems.  The detection of Gravitational waves from BHNS events may provide conclusive evidence of the existence of binary black hole and binary neutron star systems with 2.6 M_sun cut-off; Furthermore, the potential for identifying the three-body structure of such systems through electromagnetic radiation may provide key evidence in understanding the role of merger events in supernova events.  The finding that BHNS events may primarily be known by their electromagnetic emission, rather than Gravitational waves, may provide a means to test the existence of neutron star systems with black hole counterparts through observations of supernova events.  The potential for identifying the three-body structure of such systems through electromagnetic radiation may provide key evidence in understanding the role of merger events in supernova events.

In reverse, we establish that a conditioned process converging uniformly to a self-conservative, ergodic Markov process also attains a distinct quasi-stationary equilibrium, which it converges toward at an exponential rate across all initial distributions. Furthermore, we illustrate a corollary ergodic theorem under specific conditions. Moreover, we apply these findings to explore a conditioned random walk on the two-dimensional grid and ultimately address a longstanding issue of Billingsley regarding the convergence of empirical measures. Our chief tool is a novel condition for uniform convergence of a conditioned process, which itself relies on a novel characterization of bounded conditional ergodicity. This characterization holds significant value as a standalone theorem. Lastly, we extend the concept of bounded conditional ergodicity to multi-dimensional walks and derive a characterization that contrasts with existing results on ergodicity in the context of three-dimensional walks. Our analysis also yields an insightful comparison with recent work of Birkner, Greven, and den Hollander. In addition, we extend the concept of bounded conditional ergodicity to arbitrary Markov processes and derive a characterization that contrasts with existing results on ergodicity. Our findings are further exemplified through the context of a model involving fragile equilibrium in demographic models and a associated problem of assessing the fragility of an equilibrium under arbitrary initial conditions. Our analysis reveals that a model's fragile equilibrium is inherently bounded in distance, albeit not necessarily convergent in distribution. Ultimately, we establish a model's fragility as a prerequisite for its capacity to attain a quasi-stationary equilibrium and, consequently, for its conditioned process to converge uniformly at an exponential rate. To better address the rapid growth in demand for Emergency Department (ED) services, policy makers are exploring ways to modify ED operations. This study investigates the effects of extending ED treatment time on admissions and length of stay. A discrete dynamic model is constructed using longitudinal ED data from a large teaching hospital. Nevertheless, in contexts where prolonged ED stays are common, elevating the target treatment duration could yield beneficial effects on admissions, even if admissions remain elevated. In cooperative systems with multiple agents, coordination enables tasks to be performed that would be beyond the capabilities of any single agent. We investigate the concept of coordination through strategic decision-making, focusing on a scenario where agents select between two tasks of varying difficulty that are randomly distributed and partially known. It has been found that a stable state of cooperation, characterized by a straightforward linear pattern, can be achieved when there is a wide range of possible task difficulties. The surge in online fundraising (or "crowdfunding") research focuses on understanding the crowd dynamics that predict the success of crowdfunded projects. Differing from prior studies that concentrated on project characteristics, our analysis takes a more holistic approach and is less dependent on the specific crowdfunding platforms being used. By combining various research methods, we explored the impact of features describing crowd behavior on project success. Through a multi-platform investigation of fundraising in online markets, our findings reveal the common crowd dynamics that ultimately decide which projects will succeed. Consistently across our analysis, the behaviors of funders are highly correlated with fundraising success. They offer more accurate predictions of project success compared to the traditional characteristics such as technical aspects, market demand, and market conditions. We also demonstrate the crowd can sometimes act as antagonists by identifying dynamics that contradict conventional expertise, and provide insights on the dynamics that contradict conventional sentiment analysis. The validation of our findings is performed by combining statistical analysis with an attention-based neural network model, confirming that crowd behavior is a crucial element in understanding fundraising success. The research is significant as it is one of the few to investigate crowdfunding as a whole, rather than taking a platform-by-platform approach, thus revealing common patterns and dynamics across different online fundraising platforms. The discovery of crowd behavior's role in fundraising success has practical applications for funders, fundraisers, and platforms to design incentives that tap into the crowd's positive dynamics, and also consider the crowd's potential to act negatively to design mitigation strategies. Ultimately, the research can help guide the development of systems that harness the crowd's collective intelligence, as well as their potential flaws to promote successful online fundraising. Machine learning (ML) based detection of network attacks has shown effectiveness when tailored to a single organisation, but combining data from multiple sources is challenging due to data format inconsistencies and privacy concerns. To address this issue, this paper introduces a collaborative federated learning framework, allowing multiple organisations to co-create and train a robust ML-based intrusion detection system without compromising their data's privacy. A key feature of the proposed framework is the ability to collect and process network traffic from various sources, incorporating feature engineers to customise the intrusion detection model, and offering flexible modelling capabilities. Comprehensive evaluations using real-world data from two organisations, Network Repository and UMass, demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed framework, yielding better accuracy, precision, and F1-score compared to conventional methods. Notably, the integrated framework excelled in handling imbalanced datasets and achieved superior performance in detecting rare attacks. Overall, this collaborative framework provides a promising solution for ML-based intrusion detection across diverse data sources, showcasing promising future applications in this domain. These precursor studies involve the analysis of two key systems: monodromy defects without supersymmetry, and a Wess-Zumino model with a defect-free ε-expansion. Building on existing research regarding codimension-two conformal blocks with supersymmetry, the monodromy defects study draws from existing results by extending their applicability to systems with any number of supersymmetries. Conversely, the ε-expansion study necessitates a fundamental understanding of conformal blocks with chiral operators in a supersymmetric system, an essential requirement for analyzing the defects. With this foundation in place, the research is poised to analytically study supersymmetric monodromy defects in the Wess-Zumino model. The resulting findings can be compared with existing results from field theory, and the unique system's specific constraints can shed light on how the monodromy defects' central charge functions behave. Furthermore, the monodromy defects' stress tensor four-point conformal block will be bootstrapped, and the consequences of this achievement will be explored in relation to monodromy defects in systems with any number of supersymmetries. Ultimately, the research will be expanded to include multiple non-abelian defects, and the findings will be established through numerical verification. The key techniques developed in the research will be discussed, including an approach to manage the monodromy defect's cross-cap contribution, and an innovative method to directly determine the conformal block with a single external chiral operator. The applications of these techniques to monodromy defects in systems with any number of supersymmetries, as well as the challenges that arise in such settings, will also be addressed. The knowledge gained from analyzing the Wess-Zumino model will be extrapolated to anticipate the analytical bootstrapping of supersymmetric monodromy defects in other systems, such as free fermions and the epsilon-expansion of the Wess-Zumino model. This study addresses the query of whether randomizing the Medium Access Control (MAC) layer, using protocols like frequency-hopping multiple access and binary symmetric modulation, can mitigate the adverse effects of interference correlation. Additionally, numerical simulations validate the accuracy of the proposed analytical expressions. Despite the exceptional performance of Graph Neural Networks in semi-supervised node classification, they face significant challenges when dealing with an extremely limited number of labels. To address this issue, a novel semi-supervised node classification method called Informative Pseudo-Labeling Framework has been developed to tackle label scarcity in Graph Neural Networks. This approach uses a pseudo-labeling technique that prioritizes informative nodes with the greatest influence on the local neighborhood to assign labels, ensuring that the labels are effective in training the Graph Neural Networks. By combining the GNN model and the Informative Pseudo-Labeling Framework, the method achieves the highest accuracy in comparison to existing graph-based semi-supervised classification methods. Additionally, the method's capability to generate generalizable pseudo-labels beyond the current dataset has been verified to be effective in the out-of-distribution and cross-domain classification tasks. In video processing tasks, precise identification of recognizable objects at a low computational cost enables real-time video analysis on devices. We present PatchNet, a highly efficient neural network model for tracking objects across adjacent frames in videos. Unlike traditional pixel-based approaches, PatchNet leverages patch-wise correlation feature learning. This novel technique extracts patch representations directly from recognizable objects, resulting in a substantial reduction in computational complexity. Through extensive testing on common datasets, including the KITTI challenge, we demonstrate PatchNet's superior performance and significantly lower computational requirements compared to current state-of-the-art pipelines. Our results show an average runtime of under 4.8 milliseconds on NVIDIA GTX 1080 GPUs, surpassing the real-time capability required for driver assistance systems.
