This paper explores the recovery of one-dimensional Radon measures on a torus from their low-frequency Fourier components up to a given cutoff frequency, denoted as Kc. The proposed method involves minimizing the total variation among all compatible Radon measures through the problem of basis pursuit in the continuum (BPC). A characterization of BPC's solution set, including uniqueness and sparse solutions, is established in terms of a Toeplitz matrix. The uniqueness and characteristics of BPC's solution rely on the eigenvalue properties of this matrix. The solutions range from a single, weighted Dirac mass for certain conditions to infinitely many Dirac masses in other cases. The number of Dirac masses in each case is influenced by the rank of a positive or negative semi-definite matrix. The positive or negative definiteness of the matrix also determines the weights of the Dirac masses as either nonnegative or nonpositive, respectively. The study also involves deriving upper bounds for the total variation of approximate solutions in terms of the regularization parameter and the spectral properties of the matrix. These bounds hold not only for the basis pursuit in the continuum but also for the basis pursuit problem in the discrete case. The upper bounds for the total variation in the discrete case can be maintained even with minimal modifications in the matrix's eigenvalue properties. The upper bounds in the discrete case are found to be significantly tighter than those in the continuum case. The upper bounds in both cases are found to be more restrictive than necessary for the uniqueness of the solutions. The study provides a numerical example that verifies the theoretical findings. The paper also discusses how its methods and theoretical results can be extended for the recovery of multi-dimensional Radon measures on a torus and in the real line. The study specifically shows that the problem of inferring low-frequency Fourier components in higher dimensions is a computationally infeasible task due to its high complexity. However, the study reveals that restricted problems in higher dimensions can be formulated as convex optimization problems that can be efficiently solved. The most efficient algorithms achieve a logarithmic computational complexity. The paper demonstrates these findings through numerical experiments. The study also shows that the total variation regularization through the basis pursuit in the continuum or the discrete case can be applied to recover one-dimensional Radon measures on a torus from their low-frequency Fourier components. The approach can even be generalized for the recovery of bounded functions on a torus from their low-frequency Fourier components. The paper discusses the applications of the study's methods and theoretical results in the context of point process modeling, latent variable modeling, and image recovery

P4 has become the standard language for configuring reconfigurable programmable switches, with the V1Model architecture being the most widely used implementation. An open-source compiler for the P4 consortium allows for syntax analysis and translation of P416 programs into hardware-independent code, but a compiler backend to map this code to V1Model switch resources is needed. A freely available compiler backend for P416 programs and V1Model architecture-based switches has been missing until now. Commercial solutions exist but come with restrictive terms, hindering research into new mapping algorithms and custom instruction sets. Our approach utilizes a hardware-aware compiler backend that optimizes P416 programs for V1Model switches, addressing the limited register count by employing a end-host flow classifier configuration to reduce resource usage. This novel method allows multiple mapping algorithms to be compared on standard benchmarking suites, contributing to the development of new instruction sets tailored to specific use cases. The research is now open to the community, with the source code and benchmarking tools accessible through a public repository at https://github.com/mcfee/p416. The compiler backend can be downloaded from the same location under the terms of the permissive MIT license. Evaluation results are provided in supplementary materials. The open-source repository includes all necessary software, data, and instructions to reproduce our results, as well as investigate alternative mapping algorithms and new instruction sets. To our knowledge, our work is the first publicly available compiler backend for the P416 program suite and the V1Model architecture, offering a customizable backend that allows research into new mapping algorithms and instruction sets. This openness is essential for the development of new ideas in the field of network architecture, as it provides the necessary flexibility to explore diverse mapping algorithms and tailor-made instruction sets. To showcase the versatility of our compiler backend, we have implemented a novel flow classifier configuration that significantly reduces resource usage. This approach exploits the limited register count on the switch by pushing host-related information onto the switch, thereby reducing resource usage. As a consequence, our method enhances packet processing speed while maintaining low overhead and thus minimal impact on end-host performance. To evaluate the performance of our approach, we have conducted benchmarking on standard suites, measuring metrics such as classification, hashing, and parsing operations. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our configuration in reducing resource usage, at times outperforming the default P4 distribution by various orders of magnitude. To further highlight the potential of our compiler backend, we have explored different mapping algorithms and evaluated their performance under diverse workload scenarios. In numerical simulations involving fluid dynamics, the Raviart-Thomas elements are widely used to approximate vector-valued variables like velocity or momentum. Nevertheless, direct discretization methods often falls short in conserving properties like momentum when transporting these variables. To address this, we introduce a novel finite element method for the vector transport equation, utilizing high-order function spaces to accurately model fluid motion. By employing a specially designed transport operator, we achieve conservative transport of the vector-valued field and provide a thorough analysis of the method's convergence properties. Furthermore, our approach is adaptable and can be implemented using existing finite element libraries with minimal modifications. To validate our approach, we present numerous numerical examples demonstrating the method's conservative properties and showcasing its application in simulating conservative solidification problems. Moreover, our method is compared to established methods in the field, including the remap technique and conservative map methods. Last but not least, we take the first step in developing free-surface flow simulations with high-order transport, laying the groundwork for future research and applications in the field. This article will examine the concept of star formation (SF) through observation, and its progression over time, offering a fresh understanding of the process, particularly relevant since planet formation emerges from it and sheds new light on the origins of life in the universe. We will concentrate on the relationship between gas density and SF rate from the global to the galactic scale. On a cosmological scale, the article will analyze how matter behaves in the vast universe, ultimately giving rise to the creation of new stars. We will delve into the conditions necessary for SF to occur in the early universe and describe in detail dust's influence on the process. Next, the article will shift to the galactic scale, where it will explore links between the SF rate and the properties of the interstellar medium. We will present the latest observations on the relationship between gas density and SF rate in spiral and irregular galaxies, followed by an analysis of the origin of this connection. Finally, the article will conclude with the implications of our findings for the early universe and the potential for SF to occur on a vast intergalactic scale. This research was carried out as part of the Consolide FINAUST research project, where the central theme is the formation of planets and stars in the universe. We will present new observational results that will influence our understanding of the primary astrophysical process from which planet formation emerges, namely, star formation. We will examine the relationship between gas density and SF rate in the vast universe, the emergence of stars in galaxies, and the potential for SF to occur on an immense, galactic-scale. We will present the latest observations on the relationship between gas density and SF rate in spiral and irregular galaxies, along with an in-depth analysis of the origin of this connection. This research will conclude with the implications of our findings for the early universe and the potential for SF to occur on a vast intergalactic scale. We will compare and contrast the processes of star formation and planet formation within our stellar system, and their distinct patterns, as well as the unique features of each that allow life to emerge and thrive. This research will provide a comprehensive overview of the field, and our findings will be presented in a clear and concise manner in multiple peer-reviewed journals. We will discuss our research in seminars and conferences focused on the themes of astrophysics and life in the universe. We will work alongside students and young researchers, encouraging them to get involved in the project through multiple opportunities including research visits, data analysis, the presentation of results, and the co-authorship of scientific articles

We re-examine a widely accepted model for complex semiconductor production lines and analyze it in the context of states, inflows, and outflows being represented by measures on Borel spaces. This investigation arises from the lack of optimal solutions for transitioning from a smaller to a larger equilibrium state with a given output measure in a specific class of measures. This issue arises because the associated Lagrangian problem involves a two-dimensional transport task with velocities changing abruptly, a challenge addressed in a related study. To solve this problem, we propose a novel dual task and prove that an efficient solution exists and can be calculated effectively. This task involves optimizing a dual function, which is shown to be a convergent sequence of task functions for smaller systems sizes. The solution to the task is also a solution to a constrained optimization problem, which involves transporting a measure with certain properties and constraints. We further investigate two alternative tasks, one based on a continuous approximation, and the other using a discretized version, both of which provide efficient solutions and converge consistently. The task functions and dual function both exhibit convergence in the natural topological dual to the space of measures. The incorporation of artificial intelligence (AI) into this task has improved it, allowing high-quality classifiers to detect attacks efficiently; however, these classifiers demand substantial computing power or memory. The scenario presents a problem, particularly when these classifiers need to operate on low-resource devices or prevent performance overload on devices with IoT or industrial applications. A novel solution to overcome this challenge is proposed by NBcoded, a light attack classification tool that effectively combines noisy data removal and efficient data encoding, leveraging the benefits of Naive Bayes classifier while reducing resource requirements. In this study, three NBcoded implementations are developed using three Naive Bayes likelihood distribution assumptions (Gaussian, Complement, and Bernoulli). By comparing the results, NBcoded shows exceptional performance in training time and disk usage efficiency while only slightly underperforming state-of-the-art classifiers, such as Multilayer Perceptron and Random Forest, with a relatively minor reduction of 2% in accuracy and F1-score. Notably, NBcoded exhibits notable success in dealing with imbalanced datasets, achieving a 98% increase in F1-score on IoT devices with Class Imbalance. The innovative, lightweight NBcoded classifier offers an attractive alternative to deep learning classifiers, with promising applications in industrial settings with a balanced or slightly imbalanced classification system. The main advantages of this tool include its minimal resource usage, reduced performance degradation with imbalanced data, and ease of use on resource-constrained devices. Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators, mating, or escaping an uncomfortable setting. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse motivations behind movement, and the resulting complex patterns of species distribution. To simplify the analysis, species are often categorized into two groups: those that move over long distances and those that don't. However, many species fall in between, exhibiting intermediate behaviors. To better understand these species and their habitats, we need to recognize that species don't simply move in response to their environment, but also purposefully navigate through it to optimize their chances of survival and reproduction. To this end, we propose using control theory, a highly developed mathematical framework, to model how species move and respond to their environment. By identifying the connections between a species' movement and its surroundings, we can gain a deeper understanding of these dynamics and how they impact species distribution and the conservation of species. This knowledge can further inform the management of species to minimize the risk of extinction. To illustrate the benefits of this approach, we will examine the case of a species that migrates regularly and is affected by a seasonal change in its food supply, but we will also discuss how to apply this framework more broadly to other species and other environmental stimuli. Ultimately, we hope to establish a simple and effective mathematical model for tracking and studying species movement. Such a model can aid conservation efforts by providing essential insights into the behaviors of endangered species and how their movements are affected by changes in their environment. By using this model, we can test scenarios to predict and evaluate the impact of environmental changes on species distribution, which in turn will help us make informed decisions to minimize the risk of extinction. Conversely, we can also use this model to identify the best strategies for controlling species movement to meet conservation needs. To this end, we will examine a hypothetical scenario in which a conservation effort aims to protect a species by blocking its migration, but we will also explore other potential applications of this model to other species and different environmental stimuli. By taking a more general approach, we can refine the model to better fit specific cases, while also maintaining its ability to accurately predict the outcomes of different conservation efforts. To verify the model's effectiveness, we conducted a series of simulations testing its ability to predict the effects of different environmental changes on species distribution. Our results confirm the model's accuracy and demonstrate its potential for supporting decision-making in species conservation. Maximizing efficient electricity usage across transmission power networks requires optimized surplus management to minimize costs.
In our study, we demonstrated the effectiveness of using quantum annealing for optimizing power networks by defining the QUBO problem and implementing solutions on both purely quantum and hybrid architectures.
The D-Wave hybrid solver and classical solvers on Azure Quantum were utilized to solve the problem, yielding hybrid approaches that outperformed classical methods in solution quality due to lower objective function values, regardless of problem size variations. Additionally, our research explored the potential of future quantum networks in addressing complex power distribution issues.

Modern artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) methods are now employed to automatically identify physics principles and governing equations directly from measurement data. Nevertheless, formulating a universal physical law using data exclusively proves to be difficult without proposing a corresponding discrepancy model to account for the theoretical-measurement discrepancies that inevitably arise. By reexamining the long-standing problem of simulating the falling motions of objects with diverse size and mass, this work highlights several critical issues that need to be resolved by data-driven methods of automated physics discovery. It's particularly demonstrated that noise from measurements and secondary physical mechanisms such as complex drag forces, can mask the law of gravity, thus leading to incorrect model development. Utilizing the SINDy (sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics) method, which involves the use of real-world and simulated trajectory measurements, it's illustrated how the assumption that each object is governed by a similar physical law can increase the stability of learned models, although significant discrepancies between predictions and observations persist, primarily due to the intricacies of drag dynamics. This research shows that employing ML/AI in isolation will often be insufficient for accurately inferring universal physical laws and highlights the necessity for further modifications. It's hoped that this comprehensive case study will serve as a reminder to researchers that experimental design, sensor selection, and noise reduction are critical and should not be overlooked in any automated discovery of physics. Finally, it's suggested that multi-agent collaborative learning of physics could offer a promising direction for future research. This approach could facilitate the detection of universal physical laws by learning from the collective behavior of multiple automated physics discovery agents that are designed to investigate diverse physical mechanisms and objects with different scales. This vision for a cooperative future in AI-driven physics is illustrated through a hypothetical scenario in which agents that study falling objects, agents that model chaotic fluid dynamics, and agents that explore high-energy particle interactions are all interconnected to form an intelligent, self-organizing network that seeks to infer the most fundamental principles of nature through distributed and autonomous means. This intelligent, self-organizing network of co-learning agents could potentially uncover the most essential and universal physical laws by exploring the most critical mechanisms that underpin all natural phenomena. This forward-looking idea serves as a unifying theme for future research in this field and may ultimately lead to a breakthrough where AI and physics converge to reveal the deepest, most profound insights into the workings of nature. Furthermore, we observed the resilience of our design in the face of real-world fabrication imperfections affecting hole variation in the taper-nanobeam system. Consequently, we were able to achieve a high source efficiency and a substantial enhancement in the Purcell factor, demonstrating the effectiveness of our method in overcoming challenges related to mode mismatch. Neutron inelastic scattering is a valuable tool that not only allows for the identification of a glass's vibrational modes near its boson peak, but also provides insight into the specific motions involved, thereby facilitating the calculation of dynamic structure factor and sound wave proportions within and below the boson peak, a technique which has been applied to various substances like silicon dioxide, boron oxide, polybutadiene and amorphous germanium. Studies on temperature-dependent boson peaks in silicon dioxide and glycerol have also been conducted. Furthermore, x-ray Brillouin scattering measurements have demonstrated that longitudinal sound wave damping in silicon dioxide and glycerol follows a soft potential model prediction, $\omega^4$, particularly in the low-frequency regime. In this thesis, the implementation of inelastic neutron scattering experiments, combined with the subsequent computational processes, is detailed. Also included are specific research outcomes, as well as a comprehensive review of relevant findings from x-ray Brillouin scattering studies. This thesis maintains that inelastic neutron scattering plays a crucial role in advancing our understanding of glass physics, a field that can benefit from continued research driven by theoretical models and other experimental methods. In particular, further investigation into vibrational mode dynamics and the boson peak of glasses is anticipated to yield significant insights and knowledge. Additionally, the development of new, more sensitive instruments, such as the INSPIDEA instrument, is expected to significantly enhance the potential for discovering novel phenomena and deepening our understanding of glass physics. Finally, the need for greater collaboration between inelastic neutron scattering experiments and other experimental methods, such as x-ray Brillouin scattering and atomic force microscopy, is emphasized, in order to more effectively utilize and benefit from complementary facilities and techniques. In conclusion, the presentation highlights the valuable contributions of inelastic neutron scattering experiments to the fields of glass physics and materials science, as well as the promising possibilities for future research and development that exist within these disciplines. To achieve this goal, suggestions for the advancement of inelastic neutron scattering experiments, including potential technical improvements such as the introduction of wave guides, are offered. Additionally, the feasibility and benefits of performing inelastic neutron scattering studies on larger facilities, such as the MBAR instrument, are explored, as well as plans for performing experiments at the MBAR instrument facility in the near future. Lastly, the potential for inelastic neutron scattering to inspire new discoveries and contributions to the fields of glass physics and materials science, particularly through the introduction of new techniques and concepts such as the application of deep learning methods, is anticipated. A microstrip-fed patch antenna designed to operate at mm-waves with broad bandwidth and a wide angle of coverage has been successfully created and tested for integration in planar arrays. The designed antenna has a significant bandwidth of 13.1%, operating between 34.1 GHz and 38.9 GHz, facilitated by the combination of a slotted microstrip patch with multiple resonances and an optimized microstrip matching circuit. Constructed using the low-cost RO3003 substrate with top and ground layers, this design accommodates simple integration with other microstrip and frontend components via top-layer microstrip coupling gap feed. The achieved wide beamwidth of 100-125 degrees is primarily due to strategically designed parasitic patches for the primary resonant frequency and inherently wide beamwidth for the second resonant frequency within the specified bandwidth, making this a highly efficient microstrip patch antenna for operation over a ground plane. The input impedance and radiation pattern observed through measured data closely agree with the simulated results. The far-field gain observed ranges from 6.7 dB to 7.3 dB across the specified bandwidth, showcasing the design's effectiveness. This simple, low-cost microstrip patch antenna with wide coverage and broad bandwidth is highly suited for integration in high-density planar arrays operating at mm-waves. Consequently, this can greatly reduce the size and weight of these arrays while minimizing the effects of mutual coupling. The produced measured results of the designed antenna are comparable with the cutting-edge microstrip patch antennas for mm-waves. The simple structure and wide coverage make this a highly versatile antenna for various applications like imaging, data transmission, and radar systems over a broad area. Furthermore, the wide beam and broad bandwidth enable the incorporation of high integration capabilities with other microstrip and frontend components, thereby greatly reducing the weight and size of these arrays and significantly reducing the effects of mutual coupling between elements. Therefore, this can greatly enhance the overall efficiency of these arrays. Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, where random errors are introduced through a noisy channel. Using reinforcement learning, we develop a constructive approach to training a decoder for correcting individual faulty measurements. This method is notably more efficient than standard approaches and can be applied even in the presence of faulty measurements with high probabilities. Furthermore, by extending our code environment concept, we are able to tackle the full fault-tolerant decoding problem, where multiple faulty measurements are consolidated into a single noisy channel. This leads to the development of a learning-based, fault-tolerant decoding algorithm, which exhibits a constructive advantage in terms of computation cost. Notably, when surface coding is used, the threshold for fault-tolerant computation is shown to be at the 0.907 threshold for random Pauli errors. Code implementations are available at https://github.com/quantum-simulation/rl-topological-code. Additionally, an extended version of this work, including additional methods, is provided in an arXiv article at https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.11316. The PHENIX Collaboration has collected data on direct photon-hadron correlations in 200 GeV/A Au$+$Au, $d$$+$Au, and $p$$+$$p$ collisions from 2006 to 2011. These findings reveal that cold nuclear matter has negligible effects on $d$$+$Au collisions. A notable disparity exists in hadron production between Au$+$Au and $p$$+$$p$ collisions. Hadrons with high momentum fractions are suppressed in Au$+$Au, whereas those with lower momentum fractions show increased yields, exceeding $p$$+$$p$ collisions. This excess, observed at large angles and low hadron $p_T$, is more pronounced for hadrons linked to lower-momentum direct photons, indicating an increased response of the medium to deposited energy. Hadron $p_T$ distributions, corrected for influence from the parent photon's $p_T$, show that the medium's response is dependent on the photon's momentum and that the medium's properties may differ between the forward and backward polar regions in Au$+$Au collisions. Using the four-momentum momentum momentum identity $p||\vec{p}_T|$, the medium's properties were found to be more pronounced for hadrons linked to higher-momentum photons and lower-momentum hadrons. Furthermore, the width of the correlated distribution, corrected for influence from the parent photon's $p_T$, shows that the medium's properties were present in $d$$+$Au collisions and increased in Au$+$Au collisions, with the change between these collisions indicating that the medium's properties were present in the $d$$+$Au collision but were minimal in its effect. Using the four-momentum momentum momentum identity again, the medium's properties were found to be more pronounced for hadrons linked to higher-momentum photons and lower-momentum hadrons. The medium's properties were also found to be more pronounced for hadrons linked to lower-momentum photons when the response of the medium to deposited energy is corrected for influence from the parent photon's $p_T$. Additionally, the medium's properties were found to exhibit a decrease with increasing event multiplicity, indicating that the medium's properties may differ in density at the beginning and end of the collision. Finally, the medium's properties were found to exhibit a decrease with increasing transverse $p_T$ of the hadron and that the response of the medium to deposited energy is independent of the angle of the hadron within the medium. In this hybrid digital-analog approach to quantum computing, any quantum algorithm can be implemented without traditional two-qubit gates by utilizing an inherent, always-active connection between qubits. Building on this principle, our research explores how digital-analog simulation can be used to study fermionic systems, specifically the Fermi-Hubbard model, using a fermionic SWAP network and a method to correct distortions. Focusing on the effects of qubit connectivity and the distribution of interaction coefficients, as well as the precision of entanglement-inducing operations, our results indicate that an optimal qubit connectivity arrangement for simulating fermionic systems of any dimensionality is a chain for systems without spin and a ladder for those with spin. This relatively straightforward connectivity arrangement makes the digital-analog method particularly appealing for fermionic quantum simulations. Moreover, to achieve accurate results from the digital-analog simulation, the distribution of interaction coefficients should be smooth and gradually changing. Lastly, the precision of entanglement-inducing operations should be much higher than the underlying digital precision used in the simulation. Our findings are consistent with previous studies and predictably yield equivalent results across various digital-analog parameters. Our study also introduces an alternative method for achieving precise quantum simulations of fermionic systems, thereby expanding the scope of digital-analog computing. This method holds the potential to be adapted into mid-scale quantum computers that combine digital and analog principles. Our code is available in the following link: https://github.com/qiao3001/Digital-analog_fermionic_simulation. A common issue in machine learning lies in striking a balance between optimizing performance and robustly handling out-of-distribution (OoD) scenarios. Certain methods rely on complex penalty terms that can either lead to over-regularization or under-regularization, primarily because of their dependence on model hyperparameters. This research proposes an alternative approach, which leverages an established network pre-trained with a strong feature representation. When used in conjunction with an MC-NMP model, this approach yields significant enhancements in optimization, generalization, and OoD handling, demonstrating robust performance across a range of challenging scenarios, including detection of skewness in synthetic data, detection of irregular shapes in George network latent spaces, and comparison of generalization capabilities with George and RND models. Furthermore, this approach shows potential in enhancing robustness against adversarial attacks, yielding a substantial 14.97% improvement in comparison to state-of-the-art techniques. Achieving the formation of intricate structures and rapid concentration of light within or through disordered mediums is an arduous endeavor due to variations in refractive index, unpredictable light scattering, and speckle noise. To address these challenges, we've developed a novel weighted-mutation-assisted genetic algorithm (WMA-GA) with an R-squared-based fitness function that enhances image clarity, precision, and rapid convergence in forming complex structures within scattering media. As a companion technology to our binary WMA-GA system, we've designed a swift, economical, and reliable iterative wavefront manipulation system utilizing an $8 \times 8$ binary-phase spatial light modulator. Both theoretical and experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed approach in constructing diverse meta-atoms and dynamic complex structures within or through scattering media with high clarity and rapid convergence. Specifically, we've achieved 99% or better image recovery for 25 distinct meta-atom patterns in less than 5 iterations. Moreover, we've applied our algorithm to construct a 3D cubic frame structure in a 1mm-thick scattering environment with an average reconstruction precision of 11 microns. To the best of our knowledge, our wavefront manipulation system represents the first implementation of a genetic algorithm assisted by a spatial light modulator, thereby facilitating the creation of intricate meta-atoms and complex structure constructions within or through scattering media. This innovative approach has the potential to reduce the iteration count by at least an order of magnitude over existing methods, promoting our algorithm to be one of the most efficient examples of its kind. Moreover, our research paves the way for the development of low-cost, integrated and compact optical devices based on spatial light modulation technology. Lastly, the associated wavefront manipulation code can be found on the GitHub platform at the URL: https://github.com/Qian-Cheng-920105/WMA-GA-assisted-wavefront-manipulation-code. To ensure transparency in our research, the detailed specifications of our binary WMA-GA driven SLM can be found at: https://github.com/Qian-Cheng-920105/WMA-GA-driven-SLM-specifications. Additionally, the 3D printing information for our frame structure can be accessed at: https://github.com/Qian-Cheng-920105/3D-printing-frame-structure. Meta-analyses that include multiple trials based on shared study participants often report correlated effect sizes.  In such scenarios, employing cluster-robust variance estimators can effectively synthesize dependent effects, however these may produce inflated Type 1 errors in cases of a limited number of studies.  In order to improve the performance of robust estimators when dealing with small sample sizes, new estimators have been developed that estimate variance within study correlations through an expectation-maximization algorithm.  In particular, the proposed estimators leverage the structure of a multivariate normal distribution model common to multiple observations within a single study.  The result is an initial empirical evaluation which indicates the newly proposed estimators outperform existing alternatives in cases of a limited number of studies.  The developed estimators are made available online along with a corresponding implementation in the metafor package for R.  Future work may focus on extending the estimators to account for additional bias variables.  Additionally the estimators may be used in weighted analyses by assigning weights to individual study correlations.  The approach may also be applied to synthesize functional outcomes such as those measured on a continuous scale.  Ultimately the proposed estimators are designed to provide improved accuracy of variance estimates and type 1 error rates in meta-analyses with a small number of studies. This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps for solving fluid and particle equations, although this can lead to biased simulations. Our multiple-time-step integration method involves adopting varying levels of accuracy for solving fluid and particle equations and combining multiple collision time steps into a single simulation time step. We test this method using both experimental and numerical data and demonstrate its ability to significantly improve simulation efficiency while maintaining equivalent accuracy. Our method allows for up to a five-order-of-magnitude decrease in computational time for simifying complex systems involving numerous particles. By adapting established techniques to reason about high-level probabilistic code, this study achieves a breakthrough in linking operational and denotational views with a proven adequacy theorem, thereby closing a key outstanding issue identified in earlier work (Bacci et al., 2018). Our results build on previous research (Messen, 2018; Bonato et al., 2019; Bonato and Messen, 2020) while advancing the field by proposing a novel and simplified calculus for stochastic lambda terms that facilitates reasoning about both individual and distributed stochastic computations. Furthermore, our model incorporates a range of useful concepts, including continuous while-loops, shared reference variables, and random input functions. We examine the core properties of our proposed model and investigate the theoretical distinctions between distributed stochastic lambda terms and other variable-based distributed lambda calculus models. Ultimately, our study paves the way for a practical evaluation of distributed stochastic lambda calculus models against established denotational and operational criteria. The proof techniques employed in this study are based on novel and efficient methods of inductive-inductive reasoning and also contribute to the field of programming languages. The formal definitions and proofs presented in this study have been implemented in the Coq theorem prover, with all relevant code and documents available online at the address https://xenonem.github.io/stlc-denotational/index.html. Imitation learning seeks to bypass the complexity of creating optimal reward functions for agent training by utilizing expert behavior instead.  The challenge lies in environments that are modeled as Markov Decision Processes, and current imitation algorithms often rely on access to expert demonstrations within the exact same environment in which the imitation policy is to be learned.  However, when this condition is met, the optimal policy can often be easily obtained through other means.  To circumvent this issue, a new framework called Experience-Based Imitation Learning (EBIL) has been developed.  EBIL treats the imitation problem as a collision detection problem, decoding an expert's intentions from their actions to reconstruct the unobservable state and reward functions from a small set of randomly generated environments.  By applying the EBIL framework to contexts with limited expert interactions, a new method called Random Environment Imitation (REI) has been devised.  REI utilizes the EBIL framework to reconstruct an expert's policy across a variety of environments and has been tested in agent training through a range of tasks, including continuous state and action spaces.  The REI method has demonstrated superior performance when compared to existing imitation learning algorithms in tasks such as kin ball tossing and a more complex project of imitating a humanoid robot's movements to play a cymbal.  The REI method has also successfully generalized across a range of unknown tasks, including cymbal playing styles, object manipulation, and human-like locomotion on a humanoid robot.  The REI method has notable theoretical and practical implications due to its potential to increase the efficiency of imitation learning through the smart use of environment. Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly and that this reduction in crimes increases with time since the original conviction.  An initial financial analysis of these results indicates the decrease in future crime could cover and exceed the expenses associated with providing treatment.  More in-depth analysis revealed treatment has a greater impact on those with more severe mental health issues and that this effect is more pronounced in certain types of crimes.  The data also indicates that crime reduction resulting from mental health treatment is linked to convictions for less severe crimes.  The research suggests mental health treatment as part of probation can lower the likelihood of future crime within the justice system, a finding the authors will seek to expand upon in subsequent studies.  In particular, the authors aim to examine the potential for mental health treatment to lower mortality rates associated with severe mental health disorders and to assess and compare the effectiveness of different treatment methods.  An initial look at the potential for mental health treatment to lower mortality rates within the justice system suggests a significant reduction in mortality rates could occur if mental health treatment as part of probation reduces future violent crime to a greater extent than property crimes.  Based on a 10-year crime outlook, the reduction in future violent crime could result in a reduction of 3.7 percentage points in the likelihood of offenders dying as a result of their mental health disorders.  An assessment of the effectiveness of different mental health treatments as part of probation reveals that providing treatment rather than imposing incarceration lowers the likelihood of future crime and death associated with severe mental health disorders, a finding the authors aim to expand upon in subsequent studies. In protoplanetary disks, it is not unusual to come across gas and dust emission substructures.
These substructures may have connections to the formation of planets themselves.
Our investigation into the AS 209 gas substructures employed thermochemical modeling using RAC2D and precise observations from the Molecules with ALMA at Planet-forming Scales project.
Our observations of C$^{18}$O J=2-1 revealed a distinct trough at 88 au that overlapped with the areas of several millimeter dust continuum emission gaps.
We observed that CO column density could drop as low as 10$^{-2}$ g/cm$^2$ in the trough and that CO column density variations were primarily driven by temperature fluctuations rather than a decrease in metallicity or gas density.
When introducing a submicron-sized dust particle into our modeling of CO, we were able to accurately replicate the observed substructures without resorting to complex disk features such as wind or highly structured dust particles.
Based on our findings, it appears that the AS 209 gas substructures can be explained by a combination of classical planetary disk architecture and a more nuanced physical environment that takes into account the unique properties of gas and dust particle interactions. 
Our results imply a more precise interpretation of the observed substructures in protoplanetary disks and a more accurate understanding of the processes driving gas and dust separation. 
Moreover, our findings highlight the significance of considering particle interactions in modeling the substructures of protoplanetary disks. 
Our investigation into the AS 209 gas substructures offers a fresh understanding of the gas dynamics and particle interactions in a protoplanetary disk, paving the way for further research into the substructures of protoplanetary disks.

For visually appealing outfits, individual garments must harmoniously fit together based on factors like style, type, and color. Current studies view visual compatibility as a straightforward'match' or'mismatch' classification problem, where each garment item is labeled as entirely compatible or incompatible. Yet, this simplistic approach is impractical for real-world Outfit Maker apps where users must identify which specific items might clash with their created outfits. To address this limitation, we introduce the Visual InCompatibility TransfORmer (VICTOR) that's tailored to tackle two distinct challenges: quantifying an outfit's overall compatibility and pinpointing individual mismatched items. Leveraging a fashion-oriented language-image contrastive pre-training framework, we fine-tune VICTOR on a wide range of fashion visuals. We expand upon the Polyvore outfit benchmark, introducing a dataset dubbed Polyvore-MISFITs comprising imperfectly matched outfits, to train and test our proposed model. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that our proposed VICTOR outperforms or matches state-of-the-art performance on the Polyvore dataset while achieving an impressive speedup of up to 67x. We further show that our model can successfully quantify compatibility and item-level mismatching on other fashion datasets with promising results. The framework of quantum resource theory has significantly advanced quantum physics, enabling the unification of diverse methods to quantify specific quantum effects. It plays a pivotal role in optimizing their utility across various applications. The incorporation of radical quantum phenomena such as coherence, entanglement, and nonclassicality has enabled their practical application. The theoretical framework of quantum resource theory divides quantum states into two segments - the category of free quantum states and the category of quantum resources. The former serves as a baseline for evaluation, with the latter holding the valuable resources that need to be optimized. The resource theory framework is centered on two core concepts: an obstruction to processing free states and an injection mechanism to obtain the valuable resources. Recent breakthroughs within the field of standard quantum resource theory primarily focus on the incorporation of multiple resources, with ongoing research aimed at developing the underlying theoretical framework. The goal is to devise a cohesive approach that can effectively utilize the vast range of quantum effects present in various physical systems. Prominently, the field has made significant inroads in the practical application of entanglement and coherence. Nonetheless, the quantum phenomenon of nonclassicality remains understudied within the realm of quantum resource theory. This thesis aims to devise an original approach for nonclassicality within the quantum resource theory framework by first discovering an injection mechanism to obtain nonclassicality from classical states. The nonclassicality obstruction is discovered to comprise both classical and nonclassical segments. Subsequently, the nonclassicality resource theory is extended to incorporate the widely-used concept of semi-definite programming within the realm of dual convex programming. This enables the application of semi-definite programming to optimize nonclassicality across various quantum channels. The nonclassicality resource theory is then successfully incorporated into specific physical systems, with a special focus on binary optical systems. Finally, the nonclassicality resource theory is extended to a range of widely used quantum phenomena, with nonclassicality coexisting with other resources such as entanglement and coherence. This incorporates nonclassicality resource theory into a range of applications including quantum cryptography, random number generation, and enhancing randomness with quantum resources. The research findings significantly contribute to the field of quantum resource theory, marking an original and pioneering approach to nonclassicality within the realm of quantum resource theory. The extension of nonclassicality resource theory to semi-definite programming offers a versatile and efficient tool for optimizing nonclassicality. The consideration of temporal contexts within knowledge graph embeddings presents a chance for enhanced performance in resultant models, and consequently, in applications that rely on these embeddings. Despite this opportunity, previous research has given it little attention, and models developed to account for time frames often show only slight improvements over their static counterparts. Rather than treating time as a variable factor, we propose viewing time as a resource-constrained optimization problem, and through a technique that involves relative temporal optimization, we can effectively utilize temporal contexts within knowledge graphs. The proposed method leverages resource constraint three-way tensor factorization to capture the temporal contexts within these graphs, and when tested on the semantic Schadenversicherung claim prediction task, it outperformed existing methods by significant margins. Specifically, it exceeded the performance of models that considered time through markov-based or phase-encoding techniques, and it compared favorably to models that it outperformed in this same task. The improvement in performance represents a percentage boost of over 10%. As further evidence of its effectiveness, we also tested the method on the benchmark dataset for the natural language inference task called SNLI, and it outperformed existing methods by about 0.25% in this application as well. Thus, it represents an enhanced method for utilizing temporal contexts within knowledge graphs, and through its application, we achieved improved performance in two diverse downstream tasks. The code to reproduce the results is publicly available at https://github.com/joelouik/RTO_KGE. The name 'RTO' in the URL refers to the method's designation. Currently, the code supports only the application of the method to Schadenversicherung claim prediction, and it does not yet support natural language inference. It is intended to extend the code to cover additional tasks in the future. To our knowledge, the method represents the first instance of successful application of resource constraint optimization to a kge. The method is thus easily interpretable, and this ease of understanding is a significant advantage in comparison to other complex optimization-based approaches. Our proposed solution, OREO-LM, includes a special layer that lets a language model work together with a knowledge graph to find the best answer, and in return, the language model becomes more accurate. By integrating OREO-LM with existing language models, such as RoBERTa and T5, we achieved record-breaking results and also got better explanations for the models' choices, thanks to the ability to infer new relationships between entities. Experimental results show that OREO-LM sets a new standard in open-domain question answering and its ability to explain its decisions is much better than other models. The project's code and data are available on GitHub. Our approach is versatile and can be adapted to various other tasks that involve using knowledge graphs, such as question answering in specific domains and natural language inference. We have developed a novel method of constructing high dimensional expanders by utilizing covering spaces of simplicial complexes. Building upon expander graphs, high dimensional expanders play a vital role in theoretical computer science but unfortunately, there are only a few constructions available that offer arbitrarily small local spectral expansion.

Our research involves presenting a probabilistic algorithm that takes an input high dimensional expander X and generates a sub-complex Y, also a high dimensional expander with infinite covers of bounded-degree simplicial complexes. The generated Y preserves X's graph structure, reducing link complexity and inherits a sparsified local spectral expansion.

We run an approximate version of this algorithm using Markov Chain Monte Carlo, employing a random walk on X's links and sampling its balls. By taking a certain number of steps, we obtain a subroutine that produces a sparsified graph, retaining X's key local spectral properties. When applied to the complete binary cube, our method generates a sparsified copy of the cube with an arbitrarily small local spectral expansion. When combined with other constructions, our approach offers a new general method for building high dimensional expanders. As a byproduct, we develop an approximate algorithm for sampling covers of bounded-degree simplicial complexes, which we believe could be of independent interest. Additionally, we modify this algorithm to produce approximate random lift samplers for certain group invariant spaces. Leveraging these results, we present a new, deterministic construction of high dimensional expanders by utilizing covering spaces of expander graphs. By applying this construction, we generate a sparsified copy of the Hamming graph with an arbitrarily small local spectral expansion. When applied to the Hamming graph, our method produces a sparsified copy of the graph with an arbitrarily small local spectral expansion. Lastly, we illustrate the potential of our approach through an example constructing a high dimensional expander with a specific set of properties. Due to its simplicity, this example yields a sparsified copy of the cube with an arbitrarily small local spectral expansion that surpasses the known constructions' performance. Ultimately, our research contributes to the understanding and construction of high dimensional expanders, offering versatile and general methods applicable to various mathematical domains. By taking a more general approach, we derive new existence results for high dimensional expanders, offering relaxed conditions for construction and thereby yielding simpler and more general construction methods. Recent advancements in language models have revealed the potential for outstanding zero-shot performance through cleverly crafted natural language prompts. However, creating effective prompts necessitates considerable trial and error. Consequently, there is a pressing need to determine which qualities of a prompt influence its efficacy. To this end, we have collected and standardized a diverse set of prompts designed for specific tasks and tested them on tasks for which they were not initially intended. Our quantitative analysis across multiple fixed choice datasets demonstrates that prompts containing answer options and those not utilized during pre-training exhibit notable performance enhancements. Interestingly, the effect of the prompt's length appears to be task-dependent. Our findings also indicate that within a group of similarly worded prompts, the optimal choice can be identified through evaluation. Through a series of controlled experiments, we have identified a prompt hyperparameter - the number of times the prompt is revised - which significantly impacts its efficacy. Our research has the potential to pave the way for the development of an automated prompt design tool. Achieving a balance between pandemic control and economic considerations is a delicate task, as modeling under specific economic assumptions often yields non-transferable results. This research investigates how implementing timely moderate measures can resolve the trade-off between medical efficacy and economic impact, and attributes this finding to the broader concept of 'economic irreversibility,' illustrating its analogy to the principles of thermodynamics. A fundamental inequality provides a framework for the implementation of such measures. A novel theoretical approach underlying this methodology contributes to the body of econophysics research. Specifically, the study's findings have significant implications for the design of intervention strategies during public health crises and the broader hypothesis of 'pandemic irreversibility,' which posits that extreme measures are necessary to control the spread of the pandemic. This hypothesis is tested by analyzing the pandemic's trajectory with varying degrees of societal restriction, demonstrating the phenomenon of 'pandemic irreversibility' when severe measures are adopted, but showcasing the possibility of 'pandemic reversibility' when moderation is prioritized. A numerical example further illustrates the practical applications of this theoretical framework, and an extensive analysis of the COVID-19 pandemic in United States, Europe, and East Asia provides empirical support for the study's findings. Lastly, the study explores the potential for pandemic recovery through a relaxed adaptation dynamics informed by the principles of thermodynamics, and evaluates the likelihood of 'pandemic reversibility' in various countries and scenarios. A notable finding emerges in terms of the pandemic's impact on United States economy. Additionally, a comparison of the pandemic's trajectory with and without external interventions is conducted, yielding insights into the differences in pandemic progression under distinct economic assumptions. Furthermore, the study investigates the pandemic's effect on various economic indicators, including gross domestic product, consumer price index, and unemployment rate, further underscoreing the relevance of pandemic control to economic stability. A consistent pattern of 'pandemic reversibility' emerges in European countries, whereas East Asian countries exhibit a borderline case of 'pandemic reversibility.' Conversely, United States is found to be the sole example of a non-reversible pandemic outcome. The development of modern machine learning applications is centered on data and is complicated by a critical issue: understanding the influence of data quality on training. The problem of pinpointing which training examples are responsible for a trained model's inaccuracies or biases has gained significant attention over the past decade. The computation of the Shapley value for training examples with respect to validation accuracy and model fairness has become a popular framework for tackling this issue. Although recent studies have made progress in computing the Shapley value for a single machine learning model in isolation, they fail to account for a comprehensive machine learning pipeline consisting of data preprocessing, feature extraction, and model training. To bridge this gap, a new system, DataScope, has been designed to efficiently compute the Shapley value for training examples within an end-to-end machine learning pipeline, particularly for a type of pipeline referred to as a canonical pipeline, characterized by a positive relational algebra query and a K-nearest neighbor classifier. DataScope's novel approach enables the computation of the Shapley value for a wide range of canonical pipeline subfamilies with near-linear time complexity, outperforming state-of-the-art Monte Carlo-based methods by several orders of magnitude. The system's practical effectiveness is demonstrated through various experiments, including the debugging of machine learning models in real-world settings. This paper delves into a Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problem for the Laplacian in a particular class of annular domains. Specifically, we examine a setup involving a larger open set $\Omega_0$, a smaller ball of radius $r$, and consider a first eigenvalue in this scenario where both the Steklov and Robin boundary conditions are imposed. We then analyze the main features of the eigenvalue and its associated eigenfunctions, as well as how the parameter $\beta$ and $r$ influence the behavior of the eigenvalue when they vary. Notably, our analysis shows that the eigenvalue can vary greatly with these parameters, exhibiting discontinuities and both limited and extensive sets of varying eigenfunctions. Ultimately, we establish the identifiability of the eigenvalue function when the Robin parameter $\beta$ is held constant. We support this finding with a separate study on the behavior of the eigenvalue when the Steklov boundary condition parameter $\alpha$ and the domain radius vary. This separate study aims to understand how the eigenvalue behaves in response to these parameters and identifies its behavior in several different cases. We conclude by exploring its local behavior near the boundary. This research extends and complements a previous study by the third author on related eigenvalue problems in closed domains. It is expected that the methods employed and results obtained can be applied to address second and third eigenvalue problems in this context. Additionally, we establish a sharp lower bound for the second eigenvalue in this scenario, accomplished through a different approach and with different final values compared to the approach used for the first eigenvalue. To validate our findings, a series of numerical experiments were conducted to analyze the behavior of the eigenfunctions and their relationships, as well as the shape of the domains based on the first eigenvalue in this context. These findings demonstrate the accuracy of our theoretical conclusions. To obtain these findings, a series of numerical eigenvalue problems were solved using the FEM. We then utilized the criteria of eigenfunction comparison to identify the obtained eigenfunctions and determine their relationships. This was coupled with the observation that the Dirichlet eigenfunctions often exhibit different behavior and properties compared to the Steklov-Robin eigenfunctions, particularly in terms of their comparison with the second Dirichlet eigenfunction. This research sheds light on the fundamental questions of eigenfunction comparison and the behavior of these functions in this particular context of Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problems in annular domains. Assuming that key parameters are slowly changing, geometrical and physical approximations are explored for this modified equation using the WKB method near critical levels and singularities, including turning points. By maximizing the correlation between the agent's navigation actions and the resulting visual transformations, the agent makes more informed decisions, effectively learning a predictive model of the environment. Through a variational generative approach, the agent learns to simulate the impact of its actions, leveraging this understanding to forecast the outcome of different navigational choices. As a result, the agent achieves improved cross-target and cross-scene generalization capabilities, outperforming current state-of-the-art models by at least 10% according to AI2-THOR evaluations. Our method demonstrates real-world efficacy through successful navigation in diverse environments, including unseen indoor spaces and continuous real-world settings. The project's code and evaluation results are available on GitHub at https://github/NavDrop.

This work presents a novel data-driven method for identifying critical incidents related to ESS performance in distribution networks. Our approach relies on the connections between sensor data streams and does not necessitate prior knowledge of the system or parameters. It also features a data enrichment component that enables the detection of incidents even when data is limited. The efficacy of this method is demonstrated through detailed case studies that focus on active and reactive power control strategies for ESS. The proposed method is capable of incident detection and estimation with an accuracy rate of 95%, as evidenced by our case study results. Further research is needed to refine the method in line with IEC 61850 standards. Additionally, our approach can be adapted for use with other advanced distribution network elements that require monitoring and protection systems. In the future, our method can be modified to predict critical incidents by utilizing probabilistic models and analyzing the transient dynamics of power systems. This research has the potential to significantly enhance the reliability and operation of modern power distribution networks. The associated software code is available on the GitHub platform under the name 'DataDrivenIncidentDetection'. It includes all the necessary functions and can be replicated by other researchers to verify our results. The main contributions of this research are as follows: 1) A new method for identifying critical incidents related to ESS performance in distribution networks has been developed. This method is optimized for use in real-time control systems and does not necessitate prior knowledge of the system or parameters. 2) A data enrichment technique that enables the detection of incidents even when data is limited is presented. 3) The efficacy of this method is demonstrated through detailed case studies that focus on active and reactive power control strategies for ESS. 4) A review of current monitoring and protection systems for distribution networks equipped with advanced control systems has been conducted. 5) The potential of this method to predict critical incidents by utilizing probabilistic models and analyzing the transient dynamics of power systems has been explored. 6) The feasibility of adapting this method to use system performance metrics and identify critical incidents has been examined. 7) All software code associated with this research is available on the GitHub platform under the name 'DataDrivenIncidentDetection'. 8) A future roadmap for this research has been laid out and includes incorporating machine learning algorithms, expanding to other network elements such as controllable loads and photovoltaic energy systems,

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. 
Our results reveal that current leading virtual agents using the original games can already handle an extremely high number of actions in a single second, yet are typically slowed down by the sluggish games to around 70 actions per second. 
In competitive testing using the optimized games, these top agents are now able to sustain speeds of up to 250 actions per second. 
The significant boost in processing speed enabled by TextWorldExpress has already been incorporated into the primary challenge used in the TextWorld competition, where it will soon be integrated into a new 'fast' track designed to evaluate virtual agents in rapid tests lasting just 2.5 hours. 
To facilitate the development of new and faster virtual agents, we also provide an advanced simulation API called TWX-API that supports simultaneous testing of multiple agents, as well as a fast data analysis tool to speed up the process of evaluating different skills in virtual agents. 
Our research's main code is currently available for free on GitHub at https://github.com/alefimt/TWX-Express. 
An online demo of the optimized games can be accessed at https://alefimt.github.io/TWX-Express. 
An open call for participating in the competition can be made through https://2022.tworld.cormorant.io/. 
An updated API documentation can be found at https://api.tworld.cormorant.io/docs. 
An online data server can be accessed at https://alefimt.github.io/TWX-Express/data. 
An updated email address for inquiring about this research can be found at https://alefimt.github.io/TWX-Express/contact. 
An updated video of presenting this research can be found at https://youtu.be/6Q4e4QXyY7E. 
An updated slide of presenting this research can be found at https://alefimt.github.io/TWX-Express/slides

A key concept called manipulability ellipsoids effectively encodes human pose data and task-dependent information, significantly contributing to teaching robots human-like motion through emulation. In this study, we establish a connection between Gaussian Processes and manipulability ellipsoids to automate the process of ellipsoid creation. By reinterpreting manipulability ellipsoids through the lens of Gaussian Processes, we gain practical insights into ellipsoid parameters, enabling us to define manipulability ellipsoids without assuming specific process dynamics. This finding empowers the development of efficient optimization methods for resolving control variability issues during teaching tasks. To demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, we successfully applied it to a industrial robot arm tasked with performing a delicate placement operation while minimizing oscillations. The results show a marked reduction in control variability, achieved in under 10 seconds. This experience serves as a foundation for exploring and optimizing manipulability ellipsoids, thereby empowering robots to adapt to diverse teaching styles and efficiently balance task requirements with control variability. A novel method is introduced for training single-view 3D object pose estimation models, utilizing unstructured, 'in-the-wild' video footage where objects are rotated. These scenes are commonly encountered and can be easily gathered (e.g. cars navigating roundabouts, planes near airfields). The combination of traditional structure-from-motion techniques and cutting-edge object detection and feature matching methods yields surprisingly accurate 3D pose estimations in such video footage. The proposed method, which consists of two stages, initially learns a canonical pose from multiple videos, followed by a model for predicting object poses in a single view. In contrast to existing top-tier models, this method performs competitively without relying on explicit 3D pose annotations during the training process. Additionally, we present a new, widely-applicable metric for evaluating 3D pose estimation algorithms using real-world images, and demonstrate the effectiveness of our method across a range of challenging real-world scenarios. The code and models associated with this work can be found at github.com/ivanorlov/svps. For example applications, including 3D pose estimation for cars and planes, visit our demo page at ivanorlov.github.io/svps. This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse within a finite time period. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is not too strongly energy-dependent and given specific symmetry conditions, we establish the same optimal blow-up criterion found by Holmer and Roudenko for solutions in an infinite domain. A previously established approach, derived by Glassey through the concavity of variance, is not applicable in this context due to the appearance of boundary terms of undesirable sign in the second derivative of variance. Our primary argument introduces a new, modified variance measure, bounded from below and concave in a way that is relevant for solutions in this particular scenario. This new variance is shown to be compatible with the original variance and to yield similar results for established criteria related to energy and scattering properties. To overcome the technical difficulties presented by the boundary terms, our approach utilizes a combination of weighted Sobolev inequalities and carefully designed cut-off functions that allow us to focus primarily on the interior dynamics of the solution, thereby eliminating the need to explicitly resolve boundary problems. Furthermore, we were also able to establish a new criterion linked to the number of connected components in the support of the solution, which in turn allowed us to extend the previously mentioned results to address the case of mass-supercritical focusing nonlinearities in the context of connected component stability. This research was partially inspired by the questions posed in the recent paper by that of C. Mercurio and P. Maris, which in turn was an extension of the results found in the paper by that of D. A critical factor in this study is the authors' and T. Zhang's previously established criteria for irreducibility in stochastic equations with jump noises. This proof is then utilized to demonstrate ergodic behavior in stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equations and includes scenarios of weak dissipation with jump degenerate noise. Similar results were also achieved for other equations with jump degenerate noise, including the stochastic Kuramoto equation and the non-autonomous stochastic Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation. All of these findings are contingent on satisfying specific conditions related to the jump noise and the degenerate noise. This research aims to enhance our understanding of the ergodic behavior in stochastic differential equations and differential equations with measure noise. This allows us to establish a connection between the group's properties and its minimal vertex degree in the power graph. Hadron-hadron collisions in the intermediate Feynman-x region (between 0.1 and 0.9) have not been extensively studied at high-energy ranges above sqrt(s) = 63 GeV using the CERN Intersecting Storage Rings. I explore a feasible method to investigate this at the Large Hadron Collider operating at sqrt(s) = 13 TeV, an equivalent increase in fixed-target energy of 40,000 times, with crucial implications for understanding the characteristics of cosmic ray showers. Accurate measurements in this region are crucial for validating theoretical models of hadronic interactions, which are currently limited by discrepancies between models and experimental data at lower energy levels. In order to make these measurements, I propose detecting charged hadrons over a wide range of rapidity using the high-rate capabilities of the ALICE detector and its ability to operate at the boundaries of its designed input, as well as employing an improved tracking system with enhanced electron identification and a reduced background rate. The investigation involves calculating the average rapidity density of charged hadrons and the correlation of their production with the rapidity of the leading hadron. In order to achieve these goals, I outline the requirements for the condition to capture secondary interactions within the ALICE detector without losing secondary particles, which are difficult to distinguish from genuine interactions. The condition is based on the concept that genuine interactions, which are difficult to distinguish from secondary interactions, should have the same characteristics and are therefore indistinguishable. This concept is similar to the principle of parity that differentiates and distinguishes events. The condition is evaluated in terms of its effectiveness under various conditions of multiplicity and is compared to a alternative method based on the concept of centrality. Both methods capture events within the ALICE detector without losing secondary particles and are used to estimate the total number of charged hadrons and their correlation with the rapidity of the leading hadron. The method based on the condition is more effective than the method based on the concept of centrality, especially in high multiplicity ranges. The total number of charged hadrons and their correlation with the rapidity of the leading hadron are compared to theoretical models of hadronic interactions. The comparison shows that the models of hadronic interactions that are used in the study agree with the models of cosmic ray showers with the exception of the model AMPT. The exception highlights the need for further study and suggests that the study could be used as a validation model to study the characteristics of cosmic ray showers. Deep learning models, specifically Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs), are capable of generating robust image representations, but are limited when dealing with orientation transformations. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel model, Orientation Convolution Networks (OCNs), based on Landmark Gabor Filters (LGFs), which can learn representations that are less sensitive to orientation changes. By combining LGFs with standard DCNNs, our OCNs can leverage the benefits of existing deep learning frameworks while improving their robustness to orientation changes. Our proposed LGFs are centered around a circular template, characterized by a diverse set of Landmark Gabor Profiles (LGPPs) with distinct orientation features. These LGPs can be viewed as distinct orientation filters, allowing the model to capture a broad range of spatial and frequency patterns. By applying these templates to the image, our OCNs can incorporate the diversity of LGPs, enabling the model to perform well across different orientation conditions. Our experimental results show that our method, when integrated with the ResNet framework, outperforms existing robust models, while having a significantly reduced number of parameters. Furthermore, our model's performance on image recognition tasks is less susceptible to orientation changes, as evident from its high AUC values. Our proposed method, with its reduced computational overhead, is a more efficient alternative to existing robust models, making it suitable for a wide range of image classification tasks involving various orientation transformations.
