We define new families of parametrized piecewise affine transformations on 2D and 3D spaces as generalized versions of the heterochaos baker map, initially developed as simplified models for unstable dimension variability in complex systems. We identify that the intrinsic encoding properties of these maps align with those of the Dyck system from the study of languages, and this correspondence serves as the foundation for an in-depth analysis of their invariant measures. Through initial investigation, we confirm the existence of two distinct ergodic measures with maximal entropy for these generalized baker maps, and also reveal evidence that the maps exhibit behavior akin to semi-singular maps with a single non-singular component. Building on this, we hypothesize that the maps possess a single non-singular characteristic that divides the space into two distinct, invariant sub-regions, where the underlying dynamics within each region display ergodic behavior under the maximization of a potential function. In the context of 2D maps, this characteristic enables the construction of a topological Markov chain, used to determine the topological entropy and establish a change of sign for the Lyapunov exponent, and similarly, the 3D maps demonstrate the existence of a relative entropy that changes sign with the parameter value. Additionally, we observe that the ergodic measures of these generalized baker maps correspond to the Dirac measures on the Dyck paths, thereby providing a simplified model for the unstable dimension variability in complex systems, particularly relevant for applications in finance and the study of fractals in continuous systems. Ultimately, the study of these maps offers insights into the dimensional dynamics of the Haar peer-group rotation sets, previously introduced by Cuntz and Edge, and provides a link between the Dyck system and the Haar rotation sub-algebras. As a result, we are able to determine the Haar dimension variability for the rotation sub-algebras, and confirm that the intrinsic encoding properties of the generalized baker maps are equivalent to those of the Dyck system, as observed in the study of topological networks. Additionally, we establish the existence of a one-dimensional representation of the C*-algebra, characterized by a twisted action of $\mathbb{Z}_2$, and further investigate the canonical morphism to the Cuntz algebras under a change in parameter value. Moreover, the study of these maps allows for the exploration of the dimensional dynamics of the Haar peer-group rotation sets, previously introduced by Cuntz and Edge, and provides a link between the Dyck system and the Haar rotation sub-alge

Following the groundbreaking detection of the Higgs boson in 2012, the field of particle physics has entered an exciting period. A pressing concern is whether the Standard Model of particle physics adequately accounts for the scalar sector observed in nature or if it is a subset of a more complex model featuring additional particles. A critical method for resolving this query involves scrutinizing extended scalar models using future high-energy collider facilities, including the potential proton-proton collider with 27 and 100 TeV center-of-mass energy, and advanced lepton colliders at various energy levels. In this research, we thoroughly examined the potential for a complex model featuring three CP components and one neutral Higgs component, relative to the Standard Model of particle physics at the above-mentioned colliders. Our findings indicate substantial differences in the production and decay characteristics of the extended scalar model relative to the Standard Model of particle physics. As a result, the distinct features of this model should be visible at the 100 TeV proton-proton collider, with decoupling possible for the 27 TeV machine. Conversely, the signs of this model should not be visible at the LHC and the lepton colliders at lower energy levels. Furthermore, the production cross-sections and coupling relationships of the extended scalar model should be visible at the 100 TeV collider, with the ratio of the coupling strengths to the Standard Model of particle physics quantifiable up to approximately 0.1 or 10, respectively. In addition, the discovery potential for this model at future colliders, including the technical requirements and challenges involved, was also evaluated. Our research offers a comprehensive basis for further investigation of the building blocks of the scalar sector in nature at the 100 TeV proton-proton collider, with the findings applicable to other advanced lepton colliders. Additionally, our study underlines the significance of the precision of the theoretical predictions for the production and decay characteristics of the extended scalar model, with the findings indicating that an error margin of 10% is sufficient for the mass measurement of the pseudoscalar boson at the 100 TeV collider. In a broader context, our research may be used to evaluate the potential of other complex models of the scalar sector in nature relative to the Standard Model of particle physics at the future high-energy collider facilities. Lastly, the distinct features of the extended scalar model should be visible at the 100 TeV proton-proton collider, with the findings indicating the potential for the model to be verified or disproved at the future high-energy collider facilities. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for tasks like text-to-speech. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to different pitch scales using a pitch-dependent dilation factor array, learned from extended duration speech data via pitch-dependent training. Secondly, a PSC-Gated Recurrent Unit (PSC-GRU) module, designed with prior speech knowledge, enhances the model's periodicity modeling and dynamic pitch control. Evaluations on the CMU Arctic, VCSO speech corpus, and speech synthesis benchmark scores confirm the superior performance of QPNet over the original WaveNet and the recently proposed Periodic WaveNet (PWN). Specifically, the system achieved the highest Mean Opinion Score (MOS) among all compared methods, with a significant improvement in speech naturalness and the ability to control pitch accurately. Furthermore, the analysis of synthesized speech waveforms shows the distinct advantages of QPNet in modeling the periodic signal component and the background noise. The proposed model has potential applications in text-to-speech and speech enhancement tasks. The open-source code of QPNet can be accessed at the repository https://github.com/AiSunYing/QPNet. Additionally, the pre-trained models of the CMU Arctic and VCSO datasets can be downloaded from the repository at https://github.com/AiSunYing/QPNet-pretrained. The researchers responsible for this work can be reached at aisunnying@gmail.com.

Recommender Systems built with Collaborative Filtering (CF), the dominant method, have become an integral part of our daily lives as consumers. However, their limitations become apparent when dealing with recommendation data due to the complexities and idiosyncrasies of user preferences. Research has addressed these challenges to a certain extent, but the rapid advancement of Deep Learning (DL) through the integration of stochastic gradient descent has largely bypassed the exploration of CF's core issues. To fill this gap, this study delves into the problems of data sparsity and item coldness in CF-based Recommender Systems, with a focus on the role of DL for data enhancement. Building on foundations from Information Theory and Physics, this study proposes a novel theoretical framework to describe the interaction between a User and Item pair within a Context. This framework lays the groundwork for a new CF algorithm that utilizes Fisher Information Measure and Context-dependent User Preferences to generate personalized recommendations. The performance of this algorithm surpasses that of existing CF and deep learning-based methods on three benchmark datasets. Additionally, this study investigates the development of fishbowl algorithms to address the issue of data sparsity effectively. As such, these methods constitute an upgrade on the existing CF and deep learning-based recommendation methods in the field. The proposed framework and methods have potential applications in various areas, including information systems and social network analytics. This study demonstrates significant advancements in the effectiveness of CF algorithms through novel mathematical formulations and theoretical assessments. As such, this research makes novel contributions to the field while addressing the practical challenges of data sparsity and coldness in CF-based Recommender Systems. The proposed framework and methods excel in performance over existing approaches, with promising potential for applications in related areas. Detecting Earth-like planets with high precision is hindered by stellar activity. Identifying novel indicators that better reflect a star's magnetic behavior is essential for distinguishing these signals from a planet's Doppler signal. In this research, we studied the spectral features of stellar activity using data from the HARPS-N solar telescope, and found patterns distinct from a quiet star's spectrum by comparing active to quiet periods. By using SDO imagery, we quantified the proportion of active areas (faculae and spots) on the solar surface, independent of previous activity indicators. These features were linked to variations in solar faculae coverage, as observed on the visible hemisphere of the Sun. Moreover, the spectral features were observed to shift towards longer wavelengths as the star's active regions rotate into view. By analyzing the solar spectral features in terms of latitude and longitude, we found that the most long-wavelength feature shifted towards longer wavelengths as it rotated westward. By comparing this pattern to the shape of the spectral feature, we were able to distinguish active episodes from a planet's signal with high precision. Using realistic simulations, we demonstrated that these indicators remain effective even at very low signal-to-noise ratios. Furthermore, the high-resolution spectral features were also effective in distinguishing active episodes even when there is no net rotational modulation. This research provides a new, useful tool for distinguishing stellar activity signals from a planet's signal, improving the efficiency of future exoplanet detections. Additionally, the findings of this study will contribute to a better comprehension of the relationship between a star's spectral features and its surface active regions. This knowledge can be utilized for the development of a new generation of computer models simulating stellar activity. Lastly, the discovery of new, distinct indicators of stellar magnetic behavior in this research could have far-reaching implications for various areas of research, including the fields of astrophysics and solar-terrestrial physics. This research will also have the added benefit of shedding light on the relatively little understood aspects of a star's magnetic behavior in late-type stars. In the near future, the study of a star's magnetic behavior through the analysis of its spectral features may become an essential aspect of a star's characterization in various research fields. This process will enable the compilation of a large database of star characteristics, as proposed in the concept of a 'Virtual Observatory'. In this research, we presented a new, efficient technique for identifying active episodes in a star's magnetic behavior by using a combination of harmonic regression and Bayesian analysis. This technique was highly effective in detecting active episodes with a high degree

To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and those from other causes at non-zero temperatures, our method involves swapping the normal lead in tunneling spectroscopy with a high-resistance lead (characterized by large Ohm values). The increased resistance in this setup significantly alters tunneling conductance, impacting it in distinct ways. While the Majorana peak persists in rising as temperatures decrease in proportion to T^(2r-1), with r defined as the exponential product of the resistance and a universal constant divided by the Planck's constant (all values below 1/2), non-Majorana-induced zero-energy peaks fragment into two separate peaks at non-zero temperatures, displaying varying conductance in relation to temperature by way of a power law. Furthermore, tunneling associated with a Majorana mode falls under the same category of universal conductance diversity as observed in topological superconducting materials with a topological gap. Our approach offers a universal method for distinguishing Majorana modes from other causes of zero-energy peaks using a simple experimental intervention. Additionally, this study investigates the diverse ways in which tunneling conductance changes with temperature for various point contacts. For highly resistant contacts, the study reveals a new relationship between tunneling conductance and temperature. The discovery of this relationship provides evidence for a non-coherent Majorana mode, which is characterized by a wide range of temperatures over which tunneling conductance increases in relation to temperature. The findings of this study may also be used to identify Majorana modes in cold systems and those with extremely small gaps. Moreover, the study shows that the use of a high-resistance lead in tunneling spectroscopy reveals the non-coherent nature of Majorana modes by distinguishing them from other zero-energy peaks induced by topological gaps, non-topological gaps, and those resulting from the interaction of fermions with a boson in a one-dimensional system. The differentiation is achieved through the analysis of tunneling conductance, which displays diverse temperature dependence for various point contacts. Furthermore, the study establishes that the use of a high-resistance lead in tunneling spectroscopy is a universal method for identifying Majorana modes even in the presence of a topological gap, non-topological gaps, a one-dimensional system with fermion-boson interaction, and other heat-driven processes. The study is significant as it enhances our understanding of tunneling spectroscopy, is applicable to cold systems, and offers a universal method for identifying Majorana modes. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that Majorana modes exhibit a wide range of tunneling conductance

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence. Furthermore, the axiomatic nature of shadows allows for the incorporation of additional natural structures, leading to the definition of relative shadows, which in turn, facilitates the formulation of an axiomatic structure, dubbed funtoriality, and, for certain functors, characterizes when the image functor on hom-sets is a functor. A criterion for funtoriality is also provided, demonstrating that a functor is funtorial if and only if its image functor on hom-sets is a functor and for any given pair of objects, the resulting mapping of morphisms to morphisms is an equivalence. Relative shadows are utilized to derive an interpretation of funtoriality in terms of properties similar to those of topological Drinfeld Yoneda embedding. The topological Drinfeld Yoneda embedding exhibits properties analogous to Lurie's target functor, and, as a consequence, it follows that the image of the topological Drinfeld Yoneda embedding is an equivalence to the funtorial extension of THH to functors from the bicategory of topological spaces to the bicategory of functors. Similarly, it follows that the image of the classical Drinfeld Yoneda embedding is an equivalence to the Berman's extension of THH to functors from the bicategory of sets to the bicategory of functors. Relative shadows also provide a criterion for when a functor is strong, and, as a consequence, it follows that strong functors are equivalent to funtorial extensions of functors from bicategories to categories. The concept of shadows is utilized to formulate an axiomatic structure, termed quasi-invariance, and, for certain functors, it is possible to derive quasi-invariance from properties similar to Morita invariance. Quasi-invariance implies that the functor is an equivalence in the homotopy category. Conversely, our research aims to harness style-specific information, extracting it from paired images to condense into a two or three-dimensional vector, resulting in a more efficient and understandable framework for style-based image editing. By representing the relationship between global color tones across paired images as a flow conditioned on the spectral characteristics of the target image, our technique proves superior to non-conditional methods, also exhibiting more predictable and realistic outcomes in comparison to frame-by-frame color grading strategies. To achieve this with improved results, our method can also benefit from the incorporation of explicit semantic information extracted from image captions. Such an approach enables the technique to be adapted for more advanced tasks such as color grading across multiple domains. This field research focuses on snow deposition dynamics by monitoring the atmosphere's flow patterns and snowflake trajectories in real time. A state-of-the-art, high-resolution imaging system is utilized to capture snowflakes in motion, mapping the flow patterns and vortex formations above the ground. Correspondingly, a high-resolution camera is employed to track individual snowflakes in a smaller sample area within the main field of view, revealing the complex interactions between snowflakes within the atmosphere. The images obtained are then analyzed using a particle tracking algorithm to record each snowflake's position, velocity, and acceleration in a three-dimensional displacement history. The experimental results are then compared with numerical model predictions to gain a deeper understanding of the collective behavior of snowflakes within the atmosphere. This study uncovers the influence of atmospheric turbulence on snowflake settling and reveals a profound correlation between vortex formations in the atmosphere and the concentration and settling dynamics of snowflakes. The research also shows that snowflakes exhibit similar behaviors to other particles in the atmosphere, including inertial particles. Nevertheless, distinct differences in the settling dynamics of snowflakes emerge when submerging them in a sugar solution, as observed in previous research. Lastly, the research explores the potential applications of this knowledge in modeling atmospheric and aqueous layers of precipitation, with implications for predicting precipitation patterns and estimating snowpack properties. The study's findings are then applied to analyze the structural properties of a dense snow layer, taking advantage of the advanced imaging capabilities and precise measurement of snowflake trajectories. The research reveals novel insights into the relationship between the size of snow crystals and the resulting snow layer properties, offering a framework for integrating the observed snow layer dynamics with the individual settling behaviors of snowflakes. This study thus lays a groundwork for exploring other particle deposition processes through similar high-resolution imaging and measurement techniques, potentially expanding the understanding of complex biological and geological systems to predictable and controllable processes. The research is expected to run over several snowfall events in the upcoming field season, with the potential to obtain many thousand hours of data, making the data set highly valuable and versatile. A fundamental theory known as active inference underpins how living beings interact with their surroundings. This theory views the brain as an efficient tool that employs Bayesian principles to create a detailed mental framework of the world and then follows a predetermined course of action to achieve a specific goal. Despite the theory's significance in cognitive neuroscience, its practical application is restricted to simplified computer simulations due to limitations in terms of processing power and memory capacity of standard computational frameworks. This paper introduces a new graphical framework that represents a multi-scale model of active inference and showcases a real-world implementation of this model using a distributed computing system comprised of multiple networked Raspberry Pi boards. This implementation showcases the collection of sensory data, processing of the data within a distributed framework, and the execution of a controlled action to optimize a desired outcome. Moreover, the paper discusses the possibilities of utilizing this model in real-world applications through the integration of machine learning techniques known as reinforcement learning and evolutionary computation, which can adapt and improve the model in response to changing environments. This paper outlines a novel probabilistic framework designed to identify the most effective combinations of treatments in cases of colon cancer-induced immune response. An Itō stochastic process models the colon cancer dynamics, whose probabilistic evolution is governed by the Fokker-Planck equation. To identify optimal treatment combinations, an open-loop control optimization issue is proposed. Simulation results demonstrating the use of Doxorubicin chemotherapy and IL-2 immunotherapy validate the introduced framework. Furthermore, the study examines the uncertainty in treatment outcomes resulting from variations in model parameters and input treatment functions. These uncertainties are quantified using the Fokker-Planck equation and the likelihood function of the involved stochastic process. Based on these analyses, a quantitative assessment of the reliability of treatment combinations is provided. This framework can potentially be applied to other types of cancer dynamics modeled through stochastic processes. Ultimately, the framework aims to identify the most efficient treatment combinations, identify the impact of variations in model and treatment functions on treatment outcomes, and optimize the timing of treatment initiation. The approach proposed in this study is versatile and can be adapted for various other cancer types and dynamics. In particular, the framework has potential applications in cases of immunogenic tumors that undergo a phase of rapid growth, as well as those of indolent tumors that evade immune response. Two real-world clinical scenarios are presented to illustrate the clinical relevance of the proposed framework. The first involves treating a colon cancer patient with an experimental combination of MeKO-1 immunotherapy and Chemotherapy, while the second involves assessing the impact of variations in model and treatment functions on the effectiveness of IL-2 immunotherapy in colon, lung, and melanoma cancers. The study demonstrates the practical utility of the proposed framework in making treatment decisions and evaluating treatment outcomes in cases of cancer dynamics. The approach introduced in this study is in alignment with the "3 Rs" principles of Russell and Burch, specifically the reduced, reversed, and replacement principles. The idea is to apply the replacement principle by proposing an alternative method for identifying the most effective treatment combinations in cases of colon cancer dynamics. The new approach involves a reversible version of the forward operator associated with the Fokker-Planck equation. This reversible operator is a key component of the accelerated Monte Carlo integration of the Fokker-Planck equation, which is used to identify the most effective treatment combinations. The Monte Carlo integration is based on a sequential programming algorithm known as the Reversible Monte Carlo (RMC) method. The PDE-based approach is outperformed by the PDE-ML method

Event identification is crucial for informed decision-making in graph data analysis systems.  Graph-based machine learning has made notable advancements lately, but detecting events in evolving networks still poses difficulties for current frameworks. Real-life occurrences typically involve sudden changes in network behavior patterns. Current methods for dynamic node representations are ineffective at capturing event-driven network changes.  To address these limitations, we propose a new approach, called DyGED, for recognizing events in evolving networks using a combination of temporal self-attention and structural awareness.  Through extensive testing with diverse datasets, we demonstrate that DyGED consistently outperforms alternative methods in accuracy, achieving up to an 8.5% improvement.  Notably, it also offers improved scalability compared to the best-performing models, along with insightful case studies that highlight its key features.  Overall, DyGED is an innovative solution for event detection in dynamic graph settings.  As such, it has significant practical applications in various real-world environments.  We also provide a method for integrating DyGED with existing time series event detection frameworks, along with a fully functional implementation of DyGED, available on the GitHub platform.  By doing so, we aim to support researchers in using this novel event detection method.  Throughout our study, the total execution time is under 1.5 seconds, making DyGED highly suitable for real-time applications.  To validate its effectiveness in practical scenarios, we examine its performance in detecting events in Twitter posts and financial transaction networks.  We observe that DyGED is capable of processing large datasets with millions of edges at an impressive speed.  To further verify its reliability, we performed a comprehensive analysis of its stability and variability, which demonstrates that DyGED is indeed an accurate and dependable approach.  Ultimately, the evaluation showcases the substantial advantages of the proposed method over existing alternatives in terms of processing capacity and accuracy.  As such, it is an essential tool for informed decision-making in graph data analysis systems.  We hope that our proposed approach will benefit researchers in event detection tasks and inspire further advancements in graph-based machine learning for dynamic graphs, which is an underexplored field at present. The solutions of the Guderley problem involving an imploding shock wave in an ideal gas are examined, with variations introduced to the gas's internal energy equation to analyze the long-term behavior of the accelerating shock. As a result, the shock wave either approaches a steady state where all velocities become zero or escapes the region of interest due to decreasing spatial distance. What happens next depends on whether the internal energy equation has a steady-state solution, with implications for the type of singular surface that forms. A steady-state solution is only possible in certain types of gases, such as when the pressure increases linearly with density, or in gases with a pressure-density relationship following a power-law with a high enough exponent. In cases where a steady-state solution exists, a steady-state density profile develops over time, with varying density at the initial point eventually reaching the steady-state value. This process involves a convergence towards the steady-state solution through a continuous progression, where the density profile continuously changes. When a steady-state solution does not exist, the density at the point of origin increases without bound as the singularity approaches, leading to various complex behaviors and different types of singular surfaces, which can even feature a time reversal point before the singularity. An extensive discussion along with relevant calculations is provided, with different approaches to determining the Guderley number considered. The implications of these results are also compared with theories such as the similarity theory and the model of a self-similarly collapsing sphere. The present study offers a comprehensive exploration of the accelerating shock wave problem, shedding light on its various behaviors and providing a thorough explanation of the different approaches to determining the Guderley number. The research also delves into the properties of the singular surface and the time reversal point, making this investigation the most comprehensive on the accelerating shock wave to date. The provided codes can be used for further studies and to confirm the research findings. The analysis concludes by proposing potential applications of these results to diverse physical problems. In the context of zero-error source coding, our investigation focuses on how much information a guessing adversary can gain. The underlying source coding problem is represented by a confusion graph, illustrating how source symbols can be distinguished from one another. The adversary's ability to successfully guess the source sequence is measured relative to its prior knowledge, with this measurement maximized over various source distributions. When the adversary follows a specific model where they only make a single guess and can perfectly match their guess to the true sequence, this measurement is known as the maximal leakage in literature and can be expressed as the maximum min-entropy leakage. We establish a comprehensive single-letter representation of the optimal normalized leakage in this adversarial scenario, along with a stochastic coding method that reaches this optimum. Interestingly, our analysis shows that both the optimal leakage and optimal compression rates are attainable by certain deterministic coding strategies, where these goals can be concurrently achieved. We expand upon the initial investigation to consider adversaries that submit multiple guesses and introduce a new metric to quantify adversarial effectiveness in sequence prediction tasks. In this case, our analysis reveals that the optimal leakage metric can be broken down into simpler analytical components relative to the adversary's skill in sequence prediction. Additionally, our findings highlight the key differences and similarities between the single-guess and multi-guess scenarios in terms of achievable rates, adversarial effectiveness, and the maximum information gained by the adversary. We validate our theoretical outcomes with relevant numerical evaluations. To further broaden our analysis, we consider scenarios in which the confusion graph is inspired by a Markov chain and demonstrate the computational challenges that arise, along with proposing a new approach to successfully establish single-letter representations of optimal leakage and compression rates in these scenarios. We also investigate the performance of coding strategies motivated by the method of coverings in the context of adversarial sequence prediction. By exploring a range of realistic technical systems from communication technology to cryptography, our study highlights the practical significance and relevance of the theoretical outcomes to various existing technologies and their potential applications. Ultimately, our analysis suggests the potential for new technologies and applications to emerge from the intersection of source coding, information leakage, and adversarial techniques within the context of sequence prediction. By investigating the fundamental limitations of these technical systems and others, our research contributes to a deeper understanding of the various trade-offs involved in achieving optimal performance relative to the adversary's skills in sequence prediction and information leakage. Moreover, our analysis demonstrates the feasibility of optimizing both the information leakage and compression coefficients through the effective application of the Shannon lemma and its implications, as well as via more recent findings in the literature

A Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm variant employs a combined quantum-classical strategy to achieve approximate solutions for complex optimization issues.  To optimize a quantum circuit's parameters, we utilize a Bayesian approach as an auxiliary routine, evaluating its efficiency in contrast with alternative global optimizers.  The proposed technique leads to considerable reductions in circuit access frequency, typically the costliest QAOA component.  The framework performs well even at slow circuit repetition rates and with minimal quantum circuit measurements, yielding a reliable energy estimate.  Moreover, we investigate how our approach handles noise during circuit operation, discovering that for short circuits it remains resistant to disturbances.  The outcome of these findings supports the use of the suggested method as an adaptable tool to exploit the mixed capabilities of QAOA within imperfect quantum devices. Theoretical research indicates that modern spatial light manipulation technologies can be employed to redirect and concentrate these polariton condensates away from their initial sources of excitation. By strategically modulating non-resonant excitation patterns, an underlying exciton reservoir is generated which sustains the polariton condensate through continuous particle replacement. The study showcases a novel optical lens system made from a metamaterial, producing an excitation pattern of an annulus rather than a point source, resulting in the formation of a corresponding polariton ring condensate. Calculations demonstrate the potential to create a high-intensity polariton ring with an inner and outer diameter of 5 and 30 micrometers, respectively. Daany is an open-source, cross-platform C# library focused on data analytics and linear algebra. Developed atop.NET Standard 2.1 and compatible with.NET Core 3.0+, Daany consists of multiple VS projects that can be easily installed as a NuGet package. This guide serves as a comprehensive developer manual, outlining Daany's features, functionality, and usage, as well as a listing of related papers. For users seeking to integrate Daany into their own projects, Daany can be installed via NuGet as a.NET package. Daany's current version 18.2.1 is available for download. I challenge the conventional view of Galileo's influence on science by suggesting that he struggled with mathematical proficiency. This perceived weakness drove him to focus on experimentation and empiricism, as well as embracing the telescope's capabilities. His emphasis on hands-on research, which is often credited as an innovative aspect of his scientific approach, might actually be a consequence of his inability to make meaningful mathematical contributions. Similarly, his extensive discussion of basic scientific principles was, arguably, an outcome of his limitations in mathematics, as they often say "those who can't do, teach." It is proposed that Galileo's scientific vision, which is typically viewed as groundbreaking, was actually based on long-established ideas from mathematicians. The main difference lies in that Galileo chose to articulate these ideas in philosophical writing, as his mathematical colleagues were too preoccupied with advancing scientific work to bother doing the same. Ultimately, it is suggested that we reevaluate our understanding of Galileo's influence on the scientific method to one that is more in line with him being a "mathematical failure" who turned out to be a significant success in philosophy. This reevaluation not only humanizes Galileo but also resonates with many modern scientists who, like him, are better philosophers than mathematicians. It is also proposed that we should recognize that two distinct individuals, and not a single "Galileo," were responsible for shaping the scientific method and philosophy. The "mathematical Galileo" and the "philosophical Galileo" are two different people, as evidenced by the considerable differences in their contributions to science and philosophy, as well as the distinct timelines of their work in these fields. The "mathematical Galileo" was active earlier and was less known, while the "philosophical Galileo" gained prominence later and is more widely recognized.
